2026-10-03

Production batch: eighteen small functions verified, one checker anomaly

Verified A production batch of twenty small file and memory subsystem functions yielded eighteen verified Rust rewrites, each passing one thousand differential trials with zero failures, and two deferrals caused by a checker anomaly in which the original is reported as finding its argument at index zero on every trial where the argument sits anywhere in a scripted table.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack effects, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Eighteen functions verified on the first attempt with no fixes needed. The batch split into init loops over heap objects, pure queries, global table resets and queries, a constructor mixing a global sequence number into an id slot, a guarded activation wrapper, flag-gated clears, a global scan driving a ten-argument engine call, a name-to-hash pool search, and a handle dereference. Eleven use a register-plus-stack convention and nine use a stack-only convention. Two functions had merged symbol names that matched their disassembly; the rest were given descriptive names.

Verified Two twin functions that scan a ten-entry global table for a query value could not be verified. Twelve dedicated probe contracts narrowed the symptom to a precise rule: the original is reported as returning index zero whenever the query value is present anywhere in the explicitly scripted table, and agrees with the rewrite on misses and on genuine index-zero hits. The rewrite returns the true index on every trial. The probes ruled out fill size, fill entry shape, junk values, stale fills, request encoding, and instruction decoding as causes; the worker source reads correctly on every path inspected, so the root cause is still unknown.

Inferred Under this anomaly a wrong rewrite that returned a bare membership flag would pass a full-coverage contract, while the correct rewrite fails one. Narrowing the contract to index-zero hits plus misses would pass but would leave the other nine indexes untested, which is not verification, so both functions were deferred instead.

What was decided or recommended

  • Both table scans are deferred with reason other and a pointer to the lane report, which holds a three-trial minimal repro and the full probe table.
  • The checker owner should reproduce the minimal case with per-side logging of the table words, the entry register and the exit register, and compare the built worker binary against the checked-in source on the result observation path.
  • After any worker change, the two table contracts should be re-run unchanged: they plant all ten hit indexes deterministically and should then pass with no rewrite change.
  • One six-line driver extension was added to this lane's driver copy only: a stack argument kind that cycles a fixed value list, for indexes that must be negative on some trials and small on others. No worker change was needed for anything else.

How to reproduce it

Script the ten table words to fixed values with the query value at index one and anything else at index zero, pass the query value as the sole argument, and run three trials. The rewrite returns the index-one encoding on all three; the original is reported as returning the index-zero encoding on all three. Replacing the fill with a uniform table makes both sides agree, in both the hit and the miss direction.

What was confusing or went wrong

The anomaly investigation took about forty minutes because every natural theory died to exactly one observation: same-memory theories cannot produce disagreement from a shared request, shifted-read theories die to the passing index-zero trial, and alias theories die to the passing miss trials. The eventual pattern, that the original reports membership as index zero, only emerged after mapping every table position with distinct values. Nothing else went wrong: the rewrite crate built first try, no worker flakes occurred, and the riskiest contract, a pool search over a fully scripted heap pool, passed immediately.

2026-10-03

An audio initialiser that reads a word it never wrote

One small audio initialiser in this batch copies the same uninitialised word from its own fresh stack frame into four fields of the record it builds, so no faithful rewrite can be verified against it and it was deferred.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small audio-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares everything observable.

What was found

Verified Seventeen of the twenty functions verified cleanly at one thousand trials each with zero mismatches. They are ordinary small routines: two entity constructors, three flag predicates, three float conversion routines, a list drain, three guarded releases and four block resets.

Verified One initialiser reads the same stack word four times and stores it into four record fields, but nothing in the function ever writes that word. The slot sits inside the function's own freshly reserved frame, below the saved frame pointer on every possible stack alignment, so the value is leftover stack garbage from previous calls, not an argument and not a constant.

Inferred This looks like a genuine bug in the original: four record fields are seeded with whatever happened to be on the stack. The game presumably tolerates or overwrites the values later.

Verified Two further functions are large floating point routines over game data tables that exceed the twelve minute single-function budget and were deferred for a lane with more time.

What was decided or recommended

The initialiser was deferred with reason other and no rewrite was attempted: reproducing caller stack garbage would need inline assembly, which project rules forbid, and pinning the value would be a fake pass. This needs a checker-level decision, not a better rewrite: either such functions stay permanently deferred, or the harness gains an explicit rule for uninitialised stack words. Until then, lanes that find a function reading a word it never wrote should defer it with the same reason rather than guess.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the function with capstone from the project copy of the executable and list every stack read and write: the four reads of the same frame slot have no matching write anywhere in the body. The frame arithmetic shows the slot always lands below the frame base, which rules out a hidden argument.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first reading looked like a possible hidden float argument, since the value is moved with vector instructions into four evenly spaced fields. Checking the frame arithmetic slot by slot ruled that out: no alignment makes the read land on an argument, the return address or the saved frame pointer. A second trap in the same batch was a conversion loop that skips one source offset; the first rewrite assumed contiguous inputs and the checker caught it on the first run.

2026-10-03

Production lane traps: a misleading mnemonic, a short size, and an unsolved float divergence

Seventeen of twenty audio functions verified first, then three lessons worth sharing: a disassembler mnemonic that means the opposite of what it says, a function that runs past its listed size in two inventories, and a float divergence on denormal-heavy inputs that resisted half an hour of probing and is left reproducible for the checker owners.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small audio-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, deferring with a reason code where the checker cannot verify.

What was found

  • Verified Capstone prints SSE predicate six as cmpnless, which reads as not-less-than but is not-less-or-equal. The two differ only when the operands compare exactly equal, which produced a thirteen-in-a-thousand failure that the checker caught and a one-line fix cured.
  • Verified The batch's large mixer evaluator continues past its listed size in both the batch list and the repaired inventory: two more stores, the epilogue and the return sit beyond the listed end, followed by padding and the next batch function. The rewrite covers the full body.
  • Verified A zero-length guard idiom recurs in float code: an unordered compare, a flags-to-register move, a mask test and a parity jump together mean not-equal, guarding a square-root plus reciprocal against zero input including negative zero, with NaN taking the compute path.
  • Unknown The batch interpolator fails about a tenth of trials, every failure on denormal-heavy table rows in one of its two modes while the other mode passes completely. The rewrite matches a strict software emulation bit for bit, minimal tables pass, and the failure bisects to a single table word, but the original-side intermediate values were never captured so the mechanism is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

  • Trust the SSE predicate byte, never the printed mnemonic, when porting scalar float compares; check equality-boundary behaviour explicitly.
  • Disassemble past the listed end before trusting any batch size, and treat the repaired inventory as advisory where it repeats the same number.
  • The interpolator case stays deferred with its failing contract and four probe scripts in the lane folder; whoever continues should capture original-side intermediates through worker-side tracing or ask the checker owners whether denormal-heavy vector math is a known gap.

How to reproduce it

Read the lane report for the batch analysis and the per-function verdict table. Rerun any verified contract with the lane's driver copy and the stock worker binary for a thousand trials. Reproduce the interpolator divergence with the probe scripts, which drive the worker directly with hand-built single trials and bisect the failing table word by word.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two self-inflicted issues: a shell append that wrote Unicode into the Rust sources and broke the build, repaired by truncating at the first null byte with a script; and two rebuilds blocked by a locked output file while a worker held it mapped, worked around by renaming the old file aside and rebuilding. The unresolved item is the interpolator divergence above: every simpler hypothesis (wrong branch, wrong address, misread opcode, uninitialised input) was eliminated by probes, and the lane stopped past its per-function cap rather than guess.

2026-10-03

A wrong stub arity passes vacuously through identical faults

Verified A contract that declares one stack argument too many for an intercepted callee makes the stub clean up too many stack words, so the original and the rewrite both return to a garbage address and fault identically on every trial, and the checker counts that as passing with no behavioural comparison run at all.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small audio functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, one contract per function, one thousand trials each.

What was found

Verified Eleven of the twenty functions are thin wrappers that move their first argument into a register and forward the rest to a callee. The contracts declared the callee's stack argument count equal to the wrapper's, which is one too many, because the first argument travels in a register, not on the stack.

Verified With the arity overstated by one word, the recorder stub popped one word too many on return. Both sides then returned into their own first argument instead of to the caller. Since that argument is a random test value, both sides faulted on essentially every trial, at the same address with the same fault code.

Verified The checker treats a fault on both sides with equal codes as a pass and skips every other comparison for that trial. One wrapper's verdict read 995 of 1000 passing with only the termination checks present; the return value, stack, heap, call and undeclared-write checks ran on zero trials. The verdict file gives no signal that nothing behavioural was compared.

SignalVacuous verdictGenuine verdict
Comparisons presenttermination onlyreturn, stack, calls and the rest
Failing trialsa handful, where the random argument lands in the mapped imagenone, or a behavioural mismatch with detail
What it provesnothingequivalence on the tested inputs

Inferred Any contract bug that makes both sides fault identically, not only an arity slip, passes the same silent way.

What was decided or recommended

  • Fixed the eleven contracts to declare one fewer stack argument for the callees and re-ran them; every re-run shows the full set of behavioural checks passing.
  • Recommended for the checker: record per-trial end states and require a floor of cleanly-returned trials before a verdict can pass, so a contract bug can never again pass through universal faulting.
  • Recommended for lanes until then: after every run, confirm the verdict lists the behavioural checks, not just termination. A verdict with only termination checks proves nothing.

How to reproduce it

Declare one callee stack argument too many in any wrapper contract and run the checker. Nearly every trial passes on termination alone; a few fail where the random first argument happens to point into the mapped image, which is the only visible symptom. The worker source shows the comparison returning early once both sides fault with equal codes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first symptom looked like a rewrite defect: a handful of trials reported the rewrite touching original code. Tracing the fault address showed it always equalled the wrapper's first argument on both sides, which pointed away from the rewrite and toward the stack discipline, and from there to the overstated arity. The same mistaken count had been copied into all eleven wrapper contracts from one generator function, so all of them needed re-running.

2026-10-03

A wrong fifteen-argument rewrite passes the checker

Twenty-five script native handlers were rewritten and verified this shift, but the most important result is a gap: a rewrite with two of its fifteen call arguments swapped still passes, because the checker's call stub records only the first eight stack arguments. The same shift also found that several handlers reuse their own incoming stack slot as scratch space, which safe Rust cannot reproduce and the checker must therefore exclude.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, running at least one thousand trials per function.

What was found

Verified All twenty-five handlers take a single call-context pointer, make exactly one direct call to an engine function, and touch no globals. Fourteen are plain argument forwards; the rest normalise a boolean, return a byte, word or float through the return slot, or pass one float argument.

Verified Five handlers write scratch data over their own incoming stack slot: four normalise a boolean into its low byte, one spills a float result across the whole slot. The pushed call bytes were reproduced exactly, but the slot clobber itself is unwritable from safe Rust, so the stack comparison is disabled for those five contracts and the exclusion is documented in each one.

Verified A deliberately wrong rewrite of the fifteen-argument handler, with two late arguments swapped, passes all two hundred honesty trials. The worker stub stores at most eight stack arguments per call, so late arguments are never compared. Two other mutants, with a wrong boolean encoding and a missing byte mask, fail as required, which shows the surrounding checks are working.

What was decided or recommended

The twenty-five rewrites are accepted, with the late arguments of the fifteen-argument handler covered by construction and an independent argument-order cross-check rather than by the checker. The recommended follow-up is a worker extension that records more than eight stack arguments per call, after which that handler should be re-verified with no code changes.

How to reproduce it

Build any contract whose callee takes more than eight stack arguments, run the correct rewrite to confirm it passes, then swap two arguments past the eighth position and run again: the checker still passes. The same procedure with an argument inside the first eight fails on the calls comparison.

What was confusing or went wrong

A contract regeneration silently reverted an intended configuration flip, so the main runs used the stronger full-discovery mode throughout; four earlier verdicts were rerun so the batch has uniform rigor. A duplicate of the lane's own runner appeared under a different interpreter and was killed after its nature was established. Throughput fell to roughly a tenth of the pilot figure under more than thirty concurrent workers, so the remaining contracts were split across two workers to finish inside the timebox.

2026-10-03

Assembling the format readers into one workspace

The thirteen finished format-reader crates now build and test as one workspace, with no warnings under the project's strictest lint set. Assembly found and fixed six abort-class robustness bugs the lane tests had missed, all of them unbounded allocations or unguarded reads on hostile input.

What was asked

Collect the workspace scaffold and every finished format-reader crate into a single workspace that builds, tests and lints cleanly on two Windows targets, with game-file tests skipping cleanly when no game folder is configured. Audit every crate for material that must never be published, review code quality as a senior reviewer, add hostile-input tests for each reader, and propose a commit sequence for integration.

What was found

Verified Thirteen lanes had finished; five were still running and were left out. One reader had to be renamed because it shared a name with an engine-subsystem crate. Seven example programs shared one filename and would have overwritten each other in a shared build folder, so each got a unique name.

Verified The strict lint set produced about five hundred diagnostics across the thirteen crates, almost all mechanical: missing documentation sections, unmarked must-use functions, and integer casts. Each cast site was read. Harmless ones became explicit conversions; value-changing ones on hostile input became checked conversions that return the crate's error type.

Verified The audit found nothing to remove. No decompiled code, no disassembly listings, no key material, no machine paths, no verbatim game data. Text fixtures were compared against the matching real game files and none appears there. The key-locating hash and offset list are the documented run-time mechanism, not key material, and nothing prints or logs keys.

Verified Six abort-class bugs were fixed: three readers inflated compressed data without any size bound, and three pre-allocated collections directly from raw file counts. Each fix got a regression test proving hostile input now returns an error. A further three panics on truncated or mis-indexed input were fixed the same way.

What was decided or recommended

Verified The game-folder tests were unified on one convention: the install folder that holds the game directory. Two lanes had assumed one level deeper and were changed. Four optional lane variables were renamed to the same project prefix.

  • Integration should land as thirteen commits, one crate per commit in dependency order; only the save-game reader depends on others.
  • Four decisions need the coordinator: the MIT licence choice, the renamed script crate, keeping the key-locating constants, and the game-folder convention.
  • Follow-up work: an iterative rewrite of one recursive table walk, unit tests for the one crate that has none, and checked arithmetic in two 32-bit edge cases.

How to reproduce it

From the staging copy, run the workspace build, the workspace tests with and without the game-folder variable set, and clippy with warnings denied, on both the host target and the 64-bit Intel target. Then run the per-crate hostile-input suites, which need no game files. All gates pass with zero diagnostics.

What was confusing or went wrong

The panic-documentation lint fires on any public function containing an unwrap or expect, including ones proven dead by validation elsewhere. Each of the eighteen sites was verified by hand before documenting the invariant, which took longer than the mechanical fixes.

The formatter turned several long match arms into blocks without trailing semicolons, which the lint set then rejected. The failures only appeared on the second target because its build cache was fresh, which briefly looked like a target-specific lint before the real cause was found.

The hostile-input sweeps start from synthetic patterns, so they mostly exercise early rejections. The deep-state allocation bugs were found by reading every allocation site, not by the sweeps. A corpus fuzzer over real files would go further and does not exist yet.

2026-10-03

A matrix routine that copies stack garbage, and a compiler trap for rewrites

Verified One large matrix-transform routine in this batch reads a stack slot it never wrote and stores the result into the object, so three output fields receive whatever the caller left on the stack; it cannot be faithfully rewritten and was deferred.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, deferring any function the checker cannot verify.

What was found

Verified Seventeen of the twenty functions verified with one thousand trials each and zero failures. They are flag-gated float updates, small vector copies, and single-call forwarding wrappers.

Verified Two functions end in a tail jump to shared code after doing a little work of their own, which the checker cannot follow, so both were deferred.

Verified The matrix routine reserves a sixteen-byte stack area, never writes to it, then loads one float from it three times into three output fields. The slot always lies below the frame, in caller-owned stack, so the values are caller residue. A rewrite has no way to observe that memory, and copying whatever the test harness happens to leave there would be a fake pass.

Inferred The stack read looks like an uninitialized-variable bug in the original code rather than anything deliberate.

The matrix routine was deferred as unverifiable, and the two tail-jump functions likewise. Sibling lanes should treat any function whose output depends on uninitialized stack or register state as unrewritable rather than encoding harness-specific residue.

Disassemble the routine and list every write to the stack between the frame setup and the three float loads: there are none, and the loaded slot is always at a lower address than the frame pointer. Any input state gives the same verdict, since the value comes from outside the function.

What was asked

Verified One trial in a thousand failed a correct rewrite as cheating. Recomputing the trial input from the recorded seed showed the rewrite read exactly the address the original read; the address happened to sit inside the original code pages, which are readable when the original runs and revoked when the rewrite runs. The mismatch is a checker artifact, not a rewrite bug. Steering wild inputs away from the code range removed it with the comparison itself unchanged.

Inferred A second, rarer asymmetry (two trials in about four thousand, only in the fulldata phase) saw the original read an address outside the program image successfully while the rewrite faulted on the same address. ShapeCountBehaviour
Forward11Pass the script arguments to one engine call and keep no result
Byte result6Store the low byte of the engine answer through the return slot
Full result2Store the whole engine answer through the return slot
Boolean coercion4Forward, but one argument carries the slot-surgery value described below
Global lookup1Resolve an object through globals, call, invert and store the answer
Jump thunk1A bare jump to the engine function, nothing to intercept

Verified The four boolean handlers reuse their own dead argument slot as scratch: the 0/1 result overwrites the low byte of the incoming context pointer, and that modified dword is what the engine receives. Since a real context address is never small, the value the engine sees is always nonzero even when the script passed false. Whether the engine reads the full dword or only the low byte decides whether the false branch works at all.

Verified One further handler passes eleven argument words to its engine call, which exceeds the checker's eight-word call record, so its last three arguments could never be compared and it was deferred rather than stamped with a gap.

  • The jump thunk and the eleven-argument handler were deferred with explicit reason codes instead of verified with holes.
  • The checker driver should restart a lost worker mid-run and resume remaining trials; two runs died environmentally with zero failures and passed cleanly on rerun.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble any of the four boolean handlers and watch the incoming argument slot between the comparison and the engine call: the low byte changes to 0 or 1 while the upper bytes keep the old pointer value, and the pushed engine argument is that combined dword. Inferred The slot reuse looks like a compiler saving one stack slot by recycling dead space, not hand-written code: it is identical in all four handlers and serves no purpose a plain push would not.

Repairing the function inventory: what was not a function

The function inventory is repaired and the scare behind the repair turned out to be a measuring error. An independent recursive-descent pass over the plain-code region confirmed nine in ten inventory entries, removed about one in ten false entries, added roughly two and a half thousand real functions the inventory had missed, and showed that the pilot report of total boundary failure came from reading the executable at the wrong file offsets.

What was asked

Verified A pilot lane had reported that three out of three sampled functions in the mid-size range were not functions at all, casting doubt on the whole inventory of about forty-five thousand entries just as it was about to become the project's work queue. I was asked to rebuild ground truth independently with recursive-descent disassembly from roots that are certainly function entries, check every inventory entry against it, measure the error by size and by provenance, verify on a random sample, and write a corrected inventory with per-function byte ranges.

What was found

Verified The descent covered about seventy-two percent of the plain-code bytes and established around thirty-four thousand functions with exact byte ranges, resolving over two thousand jump tables along the way. Against it, the inventory sorted as follows: about thirty-nine thousand entries confirmed with the exact size, around six hundred confirmed with a corrected size, a few hundred thunks and weak gap confirmations kept, and about four and a half thousand rejected. The rejected entries were mostly jump-table case labels mistaken for functions, mid-function over-splits, data and padding, a small number of mid-instruction starts, and a handful of zero-size seed artefacts. Entries where the two analyses agreed were confirmed at over ninety-seven percent; pointer-seeded entries failed at around one in four, which is where nearly all the false entries lived.

Verified The pilot's three cases evaporated. At the correct file offsets all three are clean function entries with standard prologues, and the reported vtable anomaly points at a valid entry too. The pilot had indexed the memory-mapped image with file offsets, shifting every read by three kilobytes, and its byte dumps match the true bytes exactly one page earlier. Its verdicts and enclosing functions are void, though its suggested rejection rules remain sound hygiene.

Verified A random sample of three hundred kept entries passed independent checks: every one is reached by a call or pointer, every path decodes to a clean end, and none sits inside another function. The corrected inventory holds about forty-three thousand functions, of which about thirty-eight thousand count as game functions for scheduling.

What was decided or recommended

Inferred The corrected inventory should become the work queue, with progress and schedule recomputed from a game denominator of about thirty-eight thousand. Referenced interior points should not be kept as secondary entries: nearly two thirds of them proved to be jump-table labels when audited. The remaining few hundred weak confirmations and approximate sizes stay flagged until decrypted bytes arrive, and the rejected entries keep their evidence so the unpack work can revisit the ambiguous ones.

How to reproduce it

Verified The lane folder holds the scripts and data: a descent builder seeded from virtual tables, script handlers, relocated pointers and discovered calls, a classifier with a gap-filling backward stream test, and the corrected inventory, rejection list and headline numbers in machine-readable files. Key counts cross-check exactly against other lanes' published totals. Re-running the builder after the unpack work delivers decrypted bytes should close the remaining coverage gap.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified My first run confirmed the pilot's three bad addresses, which looked like a bug in my own file mapping until raw byte dumps showed clean prologues and exposed the pilot's offset error instead. I also briefly kept referenced interior points as secondary entries before auditing showed most were jump-table labels, and two verification failures turned out to be a noreturn-call padding idiom my checker counted too strictly. A gap-filling script failed once on an indentation error and was rerun with no data lost.

Second pilot, lane 11: medium functions (250 to 600 bytes)

Three of four sampled medium functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent to the originals with the differential checker, at about thirteen minutes per verified function; the fourth was deferred for three compounding gaps in the checker. The pilot's main lesson is that input staging, not writing Rust, dominates the work: two of the three verifications only became strong after planting controlled pointer chains through the harness.

What was asked

Rewrite four randomly sampled medium game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original, recording honest timings including failures. Each rewrite runs against the original from identical starting state over at least one thousand trials, with outgoing calls intercepted and answered by script.

What was found

  • Verified An audio voice refresh over hundreds of slots passed six hundred clean trials, and a deliberately introduced off-by-one was caught by the return check.
  • Verified A helicopter hardpoint setup passed one thousand trials with real intercepted calls only after heap pointers were planted into its global table through a worker input form the stock driver never sends.
  • Verified A vector blend routine with floating point math matched bit-exactly on one thousand trials, including edge floats and negative indexes.
  • Verified A leaderboard row walk was deferred: it needs virtual-call interception, callee memory effects for a filled-in frame struct, and per-callee scripted answers, and the checker has none of the three.

Audio voice refresh1903Verified
Helicopter hardpoints2000Verified

Leaderboard row walk60 probeDeferred

Verified Faulting trials only compare the fault code, never the fault address, so a subtly wrong rewrite passed one hundred faulting trials silently. Identical fault addresses were counted separately as coverage and caught a real addressing bug.

Verified Two trials failed as false cheating reports: the rewrite made the same legitimate data reads as the original, but the reads landed in original code pages, which are revoked while the rewrite runs.

What was decided or recommended

  • Count verified functions with their strength stated: clean-trial passes prove far more than fault-only passes, and the two should never share one number without qualification.
  • Fold the lane's driver additions back: pinned input words, planted global values, and per-run coverage including fault-address agreement.
  • The checker needs per-callee scripted answers, virtual-call interception, callee memory effects for out-parameters, fault-address comparison, and a narrower cheating rule before harder functions can be scheduled with confidence.
  • One rewrite differs from the original only in a dead spill to a popped argument slot, which no caller can observe; the stack check was excluded for that contract with the evidence run kept.

How to reproduce it

Copy the checker driver and runtime into a lane folder, write one contract per function describing its calling convention, inputs, heap layout and expected calls, stage any pointer chains the function walks, build the rewrite crate for 32-bit, and run the driver. The lane's contracts, rewrites and verdict files carry the exact inputs and counts.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • A pinned-input block overlapped a planted pointer and nulled it; the run passed vacuously on faults until the zero clean-trial count gave it away.
  • A file-reading helper returned plausible-looking bytes for a zero-filled region past the section's stored data, sending the analysis down a wrong path until a direct scan corrected it.
  • One build took over two minutes under shared build-folder contention with other lanes, and large staged inputs serialize slowly per trial; both belong in schedule estimates.

Second pilot, lane 09: medium functions (250 to 600 bytes)

Two of four sampled medium functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-identical to the originals over 1200 trials each; the other two were deferred with precise blockers. The main surprise was a seed-bias bug in the checker's random global fill that made one function's deep paths run on 6 percent of trials, found by a coverage audit and fixed in the lane's worker copy.

What was asked

Rewrite four randomly sampled medium game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, recording honest timings including failures. Each rewrite runs against the original from identical starting state over at least 1000 trials with edge values, with outgoing calls intercepted and answered by script.

What was found

Verified A main-loop table refresh with nine call sites, including two atomic operating-system calls, passed 1200 of 1200 trials on the second attempt, and a deliberately introduced mutant was caught.

Verified A script proximity tracker built on single-precision vector math passed 1200 of 1200 trials with bit-exact floating point, including not-a-number, infinities, subnormals and signed zeroes, after input shaping and a worker fix described below.

Verified The two remaining functions cannot be verified with the current checker: one executes a heap-resident callback through two register-indirect call sites the checker cannot intercept, and the other is driven throughout by eight register-indirect virtual calls plus thread-local-storage reads.

Verified A coverage audit of the proximity tracker showed only 1 in 200 fresh trials reached its deep logic. Bisecting this exposed a checker bug: the per-trial random fill for globals seeds its generator with the trial number directly, so consecutive trials produce near-identical values and global-driven branches go one way on nearly every trial. Mixing the seed first restored uniform fills and took deep-path coverage to 64 in 200 across every input kind.

Two pilots, 130 functions: what the rewrite rate really is

Thirty lanes rewrote 130 original functions in Rust under a stopwatch and tried to prove each one against the original. Small functions go quickly and mostly verify. Large ones do not verify at all yet, and the reason is the checker, not the rewriting. This entry is the coordinator's summary; each lane's own entry has the detail.

What was asked

Measure, before committing the whole swarm to it, how long one verified rewrite takes and how often it succeeds. The first pilot used fifty tiny functions chosen because they make no calls. The second used eighty functions sampled at random in five size tiers, with no filtering for difficulty, and the new checker.

Verified Almost no rewrite was wrong. Across both pilots, failed attempts were nearly all mistakes in the test set-up: a contract naming the wrong global, a driver bug, an input model that was too narrow. Lanes report first-attempt passes for most functions once the contract was right.

Verified Understanding is fast even for big functions. Lanes read and described 500-instruction functions in five to ten minutes. What they could not do was check them.

Verified Every deferral above the small tiers traced to the same short list of things the checker cannot yet do: follow calls made through a register or an object's function table, give each callee its own scripted answer, let a scripted callee write its result through a pointer, compare pointers that refer to the same place on both sides, and supply thread-local state. A separate lane measured the whole program against that list: 53% of game functions are checkable as the checker stands, but they hold only 17% of the code bytes. Per-callee answers and call interception together would raise that to 96% of functions.

What was decided or recommended

Production started on the part that works: fifty lanes are rewriting native handlers and small functions now. The checker upgrade runs beside them as its own lane, since it gates half of the code. The schedule estimate published in the chat was built from this table: days for the small and medium functions, with the large ones waiting on the checker.

How to reproduce it

Each pilot lane's scratch folder holds its results file with per-function timings, its contracts and its rewrite crate. Re-running a lane's driver over its contracts reproduces its verdicts.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three defects were found in the checker itself by lanes using it: random fills for global data were nearly constant because of how the generator was seeded, so tests of functions reading globals were weaker than they looked; a call with more than eight arguments left the stack pointer wrong; and after a trial in which only the rewrite faulted, later trials in the same worker saw corrupted state. None is known to have passed a wrong rewrite, but every verdict issued before the fixes will be re-run under the upgraded checker before it counts.

One lane reported that all three of its large functions were not functions at all and that the inventory was badly wrong. The inventory repair lane traced that to the reporting lane's own address arithmetic: it had read the file at the wrong position. The inventory's real error rate is being measured separately; the alarming number was an artefact. The coordinator repeated the claim to the project owner before it was checked, which was a mistake.

Lanes sharing one build output folder overwrote each other's libraries when two crates had the same name, and fifty lanes building at once queued on one lock. Production lanes now build into a folder each. Three times a lane wrote working files into the repository root instead of its scratch folder; they were moved out and nothing was committed.

Timings are the lanes' own and are rough: several lanes' stated minutes do not add up to their wall-clock time, in both directions. The table uses ranges for that reason.

The rewrite order: levels, clusters and what the checker can take today

Bottom-up rewrite order is computed: every function sits on one of 45 levels, level zero alone holds over fifteen thousand game functions, and just over half of all game functions are checkable with the checker as it stands today. Verified

What was asked

Work out the order in which the executable's functions should be rewritten, and how many the checker can verify today. That meant building the complete direct call graph from the Ghidra pairs plus a fresh instruction scan, condensing it into strongly connected components, assigning every function a bottom-up level, classifying every game function as checkable now, checkable after a named checker extension, or needing the running game, folding byte-identical duplicates, histogramming sizes, and packing the queue into batches of twenty to forty functions.

What was found

The union graph has about seventy-three thousand edges over some forty-five thousand functions. Verified The fresh scan independently re-found nearly ninety-eight percent of the usable Ghidra edges and added about fifteen thousand more, mostly from callers the Ghidra pass had not covered yet.

Condensation gives about forty-five thousand components, of which only thirty-five hold more than one function, and the longest dependency chain is forty-five levels deep. Verified The two large mutual recursion clusters hold about a hundred and about sixty functions each, mix several subsystems, and are confirmed by both edge sources, so they are real cycles that must be rewritten as units. Level zero holds over nineteen thousand functions in total, of which fifteen thousand are game code, so rewriting can start wide; the top eleven levels together hold only about a hundred functions.

The byte shares matter more than the counts: the as-is half is mostly small leaf functions, while the extension bucket holds three quarters of all game bytes. Verified The three named extensions unlock the middle bucket in this order, each count marginal to the ones before it:

The running-game bucket is almost entirely functions using processor-local storage or structured exception handling, plus a few dozen using operating system traps or timing instructions. Verified No game function reads its own code bytes or modifies itself, and none uses locked atomic instructions; atomicity goes through imported operating system functions instead. Verified

Two findings shape the schedule. First, about ten thousand game functions call into the still-encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so their callees can be stubbed but their calling conventions cannot be read yet. Verified Second, duplicate folding finds four hundred forty-five groups of byte-identical functions covering over five thousand functions, nearly all tiny template-like bodies, saving about four thousand seven hundred rewrites. Verified

Sizes are heavily skewed: three quarters of game functions are under one hundred fifty bytes but hold under a fifth of the bytes, while one hundred giants over four thousand bytes hold nearly a tenth. Verified The queue packs into one thousand one hundred eighty batches of twenty-nine to thirty-one functions each, grouped by subsystem and class and level-adjacent in the call graph. Verified

What was decided or recommended

  • Dispatch the rewrite queue in level order using the per-function level map, so callees exist before their callers; start with the wide, small level zero.

  • Treat each mutual recursion cluster as one rewrite unit rather than splitting it across lanes.

  • Build the three checker extensions in per-callee, indirect-call, custom-convention order, which reaches ninety-six percent checkable.

  • Fold duplicates before dispatching: each group needs one rewrite, not one per copy.

  • Plan contract authoring for the ten thousand functions calling encrypted callees around inference or a decrypted image, since conventions there cannot be read from bytes.

How to reproduce it

Take the function inventory, the Ghidra caller-callee pairs, the virtual table list, and the checker capability notes as inputs. Disassemble every function outside the encrypted range with capstone using the inventory boundaries, collect direct call targets and the instruction feature flags, and union the found edges with the Ghidra pairs. Run an iterative Tarjan pass for components, assign levels by longest path over the condensation, classify each game function against the checker rules, hash masked bytes for duplicates, and pack batches by subsystem, class, and level. The lane reran this pipeline end to end several times; the scripts and their JSON outputs sit together in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

The disassembler reports resolved absolute call targets rather than raw relative offsets, and the first scan double-added them, producing a hundred thousand bogus edges that agreed with Ghidra in only two cases. Verified Comparing five known edges by hand exposed it in minutes.

Jump tables live inline in the code section here, so the first code-read rule flagged over sixteen hundred innocent functions as self-inspecting. Restricting the rule to pure absolute reads cleared all of them. Verified

Two smaller traps: some mnemonic names are shared between string instructions and vector instructions and can only be told apart by operand shape, and the tool folds repeat and lock prefixes into the mnemonic text, which hid both string instructions and any locked atomics until the matcher was fixed. A renamed loop variable then shadowed the image base and broke a whole rescan; the per-function error field caught it immediately. The final surprise was genuine: there really are no locked atomic instructions anywhere in the scanned code. Verified

What was asked

Rewrite five original game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, recording honest per-function timings including failures. The five were a random sample of small functions that make calls, spread across subsystems, each given only with size, subsystem guess, and a callee list. What was found

Verified The audio state machine verified: four states driven by one state byte, two intercepted callees, one thousand trials with the state byte cycled through eight values including edges, all exactly compared, zero failures, and the subtle mutant caught through the heap comparison.

Verified Three of the remaining four are blocked by uninterceptable indirect calls. Two make virtual calls through object tables, which the checker cannot patch to its recorder stubs. One calls through callback hooks held in plain data globals, which are not imports, so import-slot patching cannot reach them either. Their directly reachable prefixes are verified (hundreds of exactly-compared trials each); past the first indirect call both sides fault identically, which the checker counts as a pass without comparing anything else.

Verified The fifth is blocked differently: it dereferences an output object that its first callee would fill in, but stubbed callees return scalars only and write no memory, so every path faults on the stubbed output before any comparable logic runs. All one thousand trials are fault-equivalent only, which is reported as such rather than as verification.

Verified Two local checker extensions were needed and are proposed for fold-back: deterministic input pokes that cycle flag bytes per trial (without them, branch coverage is one-in-256 luck), and a per-run histogram of trial outcomes, because a bare pass hides how many trials were exactly compared versus vacuously fault-equivalent. A third extension adds rewrite-side helpers for callees that take their first argument in a register; six of the sample's nine direct callees need it.

What was asked

Rewrite two randomly sampled very large game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent with the differential checker, recording honest timings including failures. Each function is roughly five hundred instructions with sixty or more outgoing calls.

What was found

Verified The first function is a message dispatcher: it parses an incoming message through a helper, then switches on the message id across nine arms, each validating and routing. It makes sixty direct calls plus six indirect ones, touches a dozen global words, and uses no real floating point.

Verified The second function is a copy-style constructor for a pooled world object: it stores a type tag, initializes about two hundred bytes of fields, and queries the source object through virtual calls, with real single-precision float math. Half of its sixty-eight calls are indirect, starting thirty-six instructions in.

Verified Three new checker gaps, each independently fatal for the dispatcher, proven by reading the checker worker source against the disassembly:

  • The fail path returns an uninitialized stack word. The worker fills the stack with an address-dependent pattern, so no faithful rewrite can reproduce the value.
  • The call log compares raw stack addresses. The function passes addresses of its own locals to callees from its first call, and any rewrite frame sits at different addresses.
  • Stubbed callees return one value and write nothing, but the parse helper's whole job is filling a struct through two pointers, so all nine dispatch arms are unreachable in testing. Running the real helper instead is impossible because it sits in the encrypted range.

Verified Two known gaps also proved decisive: indirect calls cannot be intercepted, so the constructor's virtual-call body would pass only vacuously through fault equivalence; and all stubbed sites share one scripted answer per trial.

All class layouts recovered so far are now one consistent set: about thirty eight hundred classes merged from the family lanes, the script native lanes, the RTTI hierarchy and the public headers, with ten thousand resolved conflicts, thirteen hundred open ones, and a draft Rust crate of three hundred forty layout structs that builds for both thirty two and sixty four bit targets.

What was asked

Combine every recovered class layout into a single set of structure definitions, resolving conflicts explicitly, and generate Rust types with compile time size and offset checks.

What was found

Verified every expected source file was present: all fifteen family layouts, all twenty two native field lists, the RTTI hierarchy and the public header names. Nothing is waiting on a missing lane.

Verified the merged set holds about thirty eight hundred classes and about eleven thousand fields after deduplication, with roughly three thousand high confidence fields and a similar number at medium confidence. About three thousand classes now carry base class links, mostly from RTTI.

Verified the draft crate holds three hundred forty structs covering about fifty six hundred fields, with explicit padding for unknown ranges and pointer fields that stay four bytes wide on sixty four bit hosts. It builds cleanly for both targets, and a deliberately corrupted assertion was shown to fail the build, so the checks are live.

Verified the largest gaps: the player object has only a handful of fields, the top level game and world objects have no records at all, physics instances are thin, and vehicle layouts are rich but about half low confidence.

What was decided or recommended

  • Inherited fields are recorded once, on the owning class. A first rule that moved fields by size comparison was tried and rejected because it pulled derived only members into their bases; the shipped rule moves a field only when two independent child subtrees agree on it, or drops it as a duplicate with its evidence transferred to the owner.
  • Sizes from the lanes are lower bounds, so each Rust struct asserts its size rounded up to four byte alignment and is documented as a prefix of the true layout.
  • About seventy observations turned out to be global variables rather than struct fields and were split into a separate globals file for a later lane.
  • Recommended next analysis: allocator and pool stride work for true sizes, a dedicated pass for the game and world objects, and targeted review of the twenty high confidence kind conflicts listed in the conflicts file.

How to reproduce it

Run the merge script in the lane scratch folder to regenerate the merged structures, conflicts, globals and moves files, then the generator script for the crate, then build the crate for both the thirty two bit and sixty four bit Windows targets. The merge log records each decision class with counts.

What was confusing or went wrong

Each lane used its own schema for sizes, bases and fields, including one off wrappers and word widths such as dword and vec3, so the first merge attempt miscounted several hundred fields until every spelling was normalised. Absolute memory addresses disguised as field offsets inflated some layouts to tens of megabytes before the globals split caught them. The first base attribution rule looked principled but was circular, because base sizes already contained misattributed bytes; spotting train only and ped only members landing in their bases is what exposed it. The Rust generator initially produced over a thousand assertion failures from implicit padding before alignment aware typing fixed them.

Replacement loader built and tested without the game

The loader that will live inside the running game and swap original functions for Rust rewrites is built, and every part of it passes its tests without the game ever launching. The proxy library forwards the full set of system library exports, the hook engine replaces functions behind individual on/off switches, and a watched control file drives toggling, bulk operations and bisecting. What remains is running it against the real game, which only the owner can do.

What was asked

Build the 32-bit replacement loader as Rust crates: a proxy library that stands in for a system library the game already loads, a hook engine written from scratch (function-start hooks with trampolines, virtual table slot replacement, import table slot replacement), a registry of replacements with run-time switches driven by a watched control file, logging with timestamps, a crash handler recording which replacements were active, and a safe mode. Prove it all with unit tests that run without the game, including a small 32-bit test program with several kinds of functions hooked under concurrent calls from several threads.

What was found

Verified The proxy library forwards every export of the system library it stands in for, with names and ordinals matching exactly, and the forwarding table is generated from the real library at build time rather than hand-written. The library itself imports only core system libraries, so it cannot load itself in a loop.

Verified The hook engine handles the calling conventions the game uses, including class methods, through small generated adapter stubs. Hooks install, call through to the original, toggle on and off, and remove cleanly, including while four threads call the hooked function and the main thread toggles a hundred times. Creating a hook on an unsuitable target (too short, undecodable, unreadable, out of range) returns a clean error and touches nothing.

Verified The readiness gate works as designed: in the test program, which has no game code in it, the loader waits, times out, stays fully disabled, and logs the whole sequence. The log from that run shows startup, the readiness checks, the timeout, and a clean shutdown with all hooks off.

Check groupChecksResult
Decoder and planner unit tests12all pass
Control file and bisect unit tests4all pass
Live 32-bit hook tests58all pass
Proxy export fidelity193 exports comparedall match
Compiler lintsall crates, both targetszero warnings

Inferred The design is ready for live testing against the game, starting with the proxy alone and adding one trivial hook at a time.

Unknown Whether the game's start-up protection objects to an extra module in the process or to patched code. Nothing in the static analysis answers this; it is the first thing live testing must establish.

What was decided or recommended

  • Exports for the proxy are declared through the linker's directive section, the same mechanism the C compiler uses. A separate definition file and command-line export flags were tried and cannot resolve the generated symbols; this is documented in the build script so nobody rediscovers it.
  • No third-party hook library is used. The engine is hand-written, which keeps the dependency list empty and the proxy's own imports limited to core system libraries.
  • The hook table ships empty. No game target is registered until its live address and expected bytes are confirmed with the game running.
  • Live testing follows a fixed eight-step order: proxy alone, coexistence with the community loader, timing calibration, first trivial hook, toggle mechanics, debugger etiquette, protection reaction, and a memory snapshot diff. Each step stops at the first surprise.

How to reproduce it

Build the workspace for the 32-bit Windows target and run the host unit tests, then run the 32-bit test program with the path to the freshly built proxy library as its argument. The program prints one line per check and a final pass and fail count with a matching exit code. Comparing the proxy library's export table against the system library's export table confirms the forwarding is complete. All commands and the eight live-test steps are written up in the loader manual kept with the lane's work.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • The proxy refused to link for a long time: the linker reported every generated stub as unresolved even though the symbols were provably present in the object files. A minimal probe showed even plain Rust symbols failed the same way, which pointed at the export mechanism rather than the code. Switching to directive-section exports fixed it on the first try.
  • The first version of the class-method adapter passed the wrong second argument to the replacement function; a live capture showed it receiving a code address instead of the test value. The stub was rewritten to rebuild the argument frame properly, and the test now asserts the values end to end.
  • A caller-side adapter turned out to be callee-pops, so calling it with the wrong prototype corrupted the stack silently and crashed later. The prototypes were fixed and a register-preservation check was added that would catch any repeat.
  • One confusing hour came from a self-inflicted cause: a probe build script left in a non-empty state made cached linker flags look like a build-tool bug. Reading the file on disk settled it immediately.

Pilot lane 10: five functions rewritten and timed

Three of five pilot functions were rewritten in Rust and proved bit-identical to the originals over about a thousand native trials each; the other two were deferred with a concrete blocker, and the pilot surfaced a gap in the leaf-selection filter. Verified

What was asked

Rewrite the last five functions of the pilot fifty in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original by native execution, time every step honestly, and run one honesty test with a deliberate mistake to confirm the comparison can catch errors.

What was found

The five functions and their outcomes:

FunctionWhat it doesOutcome
Bucket mappermaps a float sample to one of eight bucketsverified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree
Float trackerupdates a timestamped smoothing state with init, predict and clamp pathsverified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree on the second attempt
Slot store and slot copywrite through a table-selected offset into an objectdeferred: the table is runtime-initialised global data
Small clearerzeroes twelve bytes and returns the objectverified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree

Verified The deferred pair reads its offset table from writable global data whose file image is unrelated text, so the game must fill the table in at run time. A rewrite can only take that table as a parameter until runtime bytes exist, and running the original against file bytes would only exercise wild offsets. The leaf-selection filter missed these because it only screens plain absolute reads, not indexed ones; the candidate pool should be re-screened.

Verified Two subtleties needed exact handling: the bucket mapper's float-to-integer step returns a special indefinite value for out-of-range inputs where Rust saturates, and the tracker's comparisons use ordered float semantics that differ from min and max on NaN. Both are covered by targeted edge trials plus uniform random bit patterns.

Verified The honesty test confirmed the comparison catches a plausible mistake: a mutant that trusted Rust's saturating float-to-integer cast failed 174 of 1020 identical trials.

What was decided or recommended

  • Ship the three verified rewrites; keep the two table-dependent rewrites parameterised over the table and marked unverified until runtime bytes or a table-patching runner exist.
  • Re-screen the leaf pool for indexed absolute reads of writable data before assigning more pilot functions.
  • Budget pilot comparisons at a few trials per second per machine with single-shot runners; batching would change this substantially.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's twin crate for 32-bit x86, then run its parallel driver: it feeds identical edge and random inputs to the original through the native runner and to the Rust twin, and compares return values bit-exactly, floating-point results bit-exactly, written memory byte-exactly, and the stack pointer after return. Machine records of every trial batch are kept with the lane's data files.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three unaligned-pointer trials for the small clearer first appeared to fail, but the original was correct: a twelve-byte zero at an unaligned address spans four partial double-words, and the driver's comparison had assumed aligned writes. The driver was fixed to compare byte-exact images and the trials re-run. The tracker's first attempt missed ten trials because the original's floating-point return quiets signalling NaNs while the rewrite passed them through; the rewrite now quiets at return and keeps raw bits in the store. The candidate record for the bucket mapper also lists a register input that its own code zeroes before reading; the rewrite treats it as clobbered, not input.

Rewrite five small leaf functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with at least a thousand random-plus-edge trials, and record honest per-function timings for the project schedule. The functions were a four-value store with flag bits, a table-lookup byte splice, a logarithm-like float helper, a two-instruction object initialiser, and an angle wrapping routine.

Verified Four rewrites agree with the originals on every trial: 4236 trials total, zero mismatches, with floats compared bit-exactly including the floating-point return register.

Verified Two smaller surprises: the object initialiser writes an address that changes when the program is loaded at a different base, so the rewrite takes it as a parameter; and the logarithm helper indexes a two-entry table with a register that always holds zero, leaving one entry permanently unread.

The first logarithm rewrite failed half its trials because the table index was misread as the input sign bit when it actually always selects the zero entry; re-reading the register flow fixed it. Build times were dominated by waiting on a shared build cache locked by other lanes.

Native handlers ATTACH_PED_TO_CAR to CLEAR_ROOM_FOR_OBJECT: what they reveal

All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled and matched against the public native database and the decompiled mission scripts. Nearly every handler is a thin wrapper that unpacks script arguments and calls one engine function, and the engine functions resolve script handles through a single shared pool lookup. Four public param counts are wrong, one documented return value never reaches scripts, and the shared pool lookup sits in the encrypted part of the executable so it could only be observed, not read.

What was asked

Recover engine names and meanings from a batch of 140 script native handlers, propose names for the functions each handler calls, record object fields the handlers touch, and note stubs, shared handlers and encrypted code.

What was found

Verified Every handler receives one pointer to a call context. Slot zero of that context points at the return-value slot and the third slot points at the argument array. No handler in this batch reads anything else from the context, and none writes back into the argument array. Twenty-five handlers return a value; the rest are void at the script level.

Verified Most handlers share one shape: read the arguments, call a single engine function, store the result if there is one. Ten handlers are a bare jump to the engine function, three are jump chains ending in a few inline instructions that flip a global flag, and two attach handlers pass through a shared second-stage unpacker. The breakpoint native is a lone trap instruction and is never called by shipped scripts.

Verified Forty-three engine functions resolve script handles through one shared lookup routine, always with the pool pointer in the same register and the handle on the stack. The same routine serves the ped, vehicle and object pools. It lives in the encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so its internals stay unknown; only its call pattern is established.

Verified The observed argument counts agree with the public database for all but four natives. The travel-distance native reads six arguments, not seven; the mission-entity check reads three, not zero; the ceiling function reads one, not two; and the event-precedence clear reads two, not zero. The decompiled scripts agree with the binary in each case.

Verified The camera-sequence progress handler calls its engine function but never stores the result, so whatever the engine computes never reaches scripts. No shipped script calls that native. Separately, three decision-maker natives share one identical handler, and the two cell-camera visibility natives share one engine function.

Inferred Field meanings proposed from single-purpose wrappers include the two car colour bytes, the last-damage bone and last-weapon-damage fields (the latter at the same offset on peds, vehicles and objects, so it sits on a shared base class), ped flag words for blocked animations and cover behaviour, per-bit player damage flags, and a stat-id range that decides which stats can carry a string.

What was decided or recommended

Engine wrapper functions are proposed for naming after their native, with the shared pool lookup, the second-stage unpackers and the pool and manager globals proposed as cross-lane shared names. The four wrong public param counts and the dropped progress return should be fed back to the native documentation. The encrypted pool lookup needs the decrypted executable before anyone can go further.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone, follow jumps to the end of each chain, record argument-array reads, direct calls and return-slot writes, and compare the highest argument index against the public param counts. Then disassemble one level down from each engine function and record which pool or manager global it loads before resolving handles. The per-native records, proposed names and proposed fields ship as JSON alongside the lane report.

What was confusing or went wrong

The disassembler prints small numbers without a base prefix, so an early version of the analysis script misread offsets and found no arguments at all until the parser was fixed. A register-tracking bug then tagged the wrong values until stack loads were excluded from propagation. The shared pool lookup initially decoded to two plausible instructions before its bytes were recognised as ciphertext, and those two phantom instructions were thrown out. A script-usage scan over the decompiled missions took far longer than planned because of per-native regex passes.

The checker: proving rewrites match the original

The project now has a working equivalence checker: a tool that runs an original game function and its Rust rewrite side by side from identical starting state and compares everything observable. It was proven on twenty small functions of mixed kinds, where every correct rewrite passed and every deliberately broken one failed.

What was asked

Build the tool that decides whether a Rust rewrite behaves the same as the original function: run both from identical state, compare return values, written memory, stack-pointer movement, outgoing calls and crashes, with generated inputs, scripted callee answers, crash and hang handling, and protection against rewrites that cheat by calling the original. Then prove it on twenty functions and show it catches subtly wrong versions of each.

What was found

Verified The checker works end to end. Twenty functions were proven: six plain arithmetic routines, four pointer-writing constructors and setters, three methods reading object fields, two global-variable readers, three functions calling other functions through intercepted call sites, and two returning floating-point values. Each ran two hundred generated inputs against its rewrite with zero failures, and each of twenty mutants (off-by-one constants, swapped arguments, wrong operators, missed writes, wrong signs, a value returned in the wrong register part) failed as required.

Verified Cheating rewrites are caught: a rewrite that reads the original code or calls the original function is reported as cheating, because the original code pages are made inaccessible while the rewrite runs.

Verified Calls into system and library routines are intercepted: a wrapper that calls through the import table was checked over fifty trials with the call recorded and a scripted answer returned to both sides.

Verified The checker caught four genuine mistakes during its own construction, including a wrong return value in one of the proof rewrites and three comparison rules that were too strict (a callee's own stack frame, scratch registers at call sites, and a misaligned global range in a contract).

Verified Throughput is a few milliseconds per trial for simple functions, rising to around a tenth of a second when every writable data section is scanned for undeclared writes. The full twenty-function proof runs in a few minutes. The host slows noticeably under sustained load, so every verdict records its own timing.

What was decided or recommended

The verdict file format matches what the work-queue acceptance tool expects, and all twenty verdicts pass its validator. Recommended next steps: per-callee scripted answers for functions calling several routines, interception of register-indirect calls, a faster undeclared-write scan, and one worker process per processor core.

How to reproduce it

Build the 32-bit worker and the rewrite library with the project's Rust toolchain, then run the Python driver over the twenty example contracts in the lane scratch folder. It produces one verdict file per function plus a summary with throughput. A second script demonstrates the cheat detection and the import-table interception.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two candidate functions taken from the earlier function survey turned out to be mid-function fragments rather than real entries and had to be replaced after disassembly showed they started with register restores. A shared build cache made one rebuild fail with an access error until a stray worker process exited. The queue tooling renamed one of its address helpers mid-task, which broke the validation snippet until it was pointed at the new name; the verdict format itself was unchanged.

  • Verified Native calls are bound when a script loads, not looked up while it runs: the loader overwrites each native hash in the code with the handler address, writing zero for unknown hashes, and the interpreter simply calls whatever address it finds.
  • Verified The thread layout derived from the handlers agrees with the layout published by the open-source script debugger on every field, with no disagreements, including the five thread states and the order of the five virtual functions.
  • Verified Eighty-two related functions were identified with roles, including the per-frame scheduler, thread reset, kill and spawn, the program and native tables, the loader, the native binder, and the game-specific thread overrides.
  • Verified The original interpreter bytes executed a synthetic program (push two numbers, add) and produced the correct stack, plus both error paths. The per-instruction budget, the saved instruction pointer and the restored globals all behaved as the static analysis predicted.

Class layouts: user interface, front end, HUD, replay editor and web browser classes

The interface family is now mapped: 78 classes, almost all of their virtual functions identified, and two surprises — every interface object carries a virtual function that returns a hash of its own class name, and the deleting destructor sits in the third slot instead of the first. About two in five virtual functions are trivial field getters and setters, so a large share of the rewrite is mechanical.

What was asked

Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the user interface, front end, HUD, replay editor and web browser classes: for each class, its virtual function table with overridden versus inherited slots, its constructors and destructors, its object size, its fields with confidence ratings, and its relationships to other classes, plus a family-wide inheritance tree, shared interface description, and rewrite order.

What was found

Verified All 78 classes were processed, covering 6,399 virtual function slots, of which 93 percent point at readable code and 7 percent into the encrypted range. 76 classes have at least one constructor or destructor in readable code. Two do not: one class has no virtual table at all, and one task-related class whose base lives in another lane's batch.

Verified The interface framework is one large single-inheritance tree. A layout root with 115 virtual functions sits at the top, a panel class adds 8 more, and around 45 widgets, menus and video editor screens hang below it, most adding nothing and differing only in which functions they override. The widest tables belong to text, layout and video clip classes with up to 149 slots. Separate small families cover the HTML browser nodes, the replay editor overlay widgets, and the play statistics classes.

Verified Slot zero of every interface table is a small stub that hashes the class's own name string; the stored name was read back and matches the owning class in 47 of 51 cases, with 4 classes inheriting another class's stub. Slot one is a shared boolean setter, and slot two is the scalar deleting destructor. No vector deleting destructor appears in any table in the batch.

Verified 42 percent of all slots are trivial accessors: 1,734 getters and 929 setters, including paired float getters that look like rectangle coordinates and dense boolean flag accessors. Only about 5 percent of slots are true unknowns. Roughly ten slots in the root table look like pure virtuals: the base entry is an encrypted stub and many subclasses override it with readable implementations, so the behaviour is recoverable from the overrides.

Verified Object sizes were recovered from allocation sites for 14 classes, including three cases with three agreeing callers each; the rest are lower bounds from the furthest field observed, with the weakest cases flagged as unknown. The panel base is about 480 bytes, the basic video clip about 768, and its montage subclass about 796. Constructor chains into base classes were confirmed throughout.

Verified The HTML node classes have single-entry virtual tables holding only the destructor, confirmed by reading the raw table memory, so their behaviour must live in non-virtual functions. The replay widget root is abstract with two pure virtuals. The statistics classes have five slots each. One upload class has no virtual table and needs string-based discovery instead.

What was decided or recommended

Inferred The recommended rewrite order starts with the tiny statistics and font classes, then the HTML nodes, then the replay widgets, then the shared interface root with its accessors and hot override slots, then the panel class, then the leaf widgets, and finally the wide text, layout and clip classes. Deferred to other lanes: the upload class, two task and network stragglers that landed in this batch, one suspicious size bound, and the slot-order puzzle below.

  • Rewrite the roughly ten pure virtuals from their readable overrides, not from the encrypted base stubs.
  • Analyse each shared implementation once: thousands of slots collapse to dozens of unique functions.
  • Mine the captured constructor string references for real field names before writing headers.

How to reproduce it

All work was done with a Python script using capstone on the readable code range only, driven by the RTTI class and virtual table inventories from earlier lanes. The script scans readable code for each table's address to find constructors and destructors, tracks the object pointer through each function to collect field accesses with widths and read/write direction, classifies each virtual function by shape, and votes object sizes from allocation call patterns. Per-class records with fields, slots and constructors are stored as structured data alongside the lane report.

Unknown The virtual table head contradicts the usual compiler order: the deleting destructor is in the third slot, preceded by the class-name hash stub and a boolean setter. Three size votes that contradicted base-class sizes or field reach were rejected rather than reported.

Class layouts: AI task classes, second half (CTaskSimple* and other CTask*)
