The main caveat is that every object size is a lower bound, because tasks come from a pool allocator that takes no size argument.

What was asked

Recover object layouts and virtual interfaces for the AI task family, second half: the CTaskSimple leaf classes plus the CTask root, the move interface, and the small task scaffold classes. For each class: which virtual slots it overrides, its constructors and destructors, its size, its fields, and its relationships to other classes, all from the unencrypted code only.

What was found

Verified The family shares one virtual interface: the root has 17 slots, the simple-task base extends it to 20, and most leaves keep 20. Slot zero holds the deleting destructor in nearly every class, one slot is overridden by almost all leaves with a small integer constant that acts as a task-type ID (99 recovered), and one slot keeps a single shared implementation inherited by the whole family. Two slots are never overridden by any class.

Verified Fifteen movement classes use multiple inheritance: each carries a second 13-slot table for the move interface, embedded one fifth of the way into the object, with a float and a flags word beside it. The animation-driven NaturalMotion leaves have the widest tables at 29 slots and the largest method bodies.

Verified Constructors were found for nearly every class by searching plain code for each class table address. Destructor identification is strong: over a hundred real destructors confirmed through the deleting-destructor call pattern. Field recovery totals 1,320 observations, about a quarter high confidence, a third medium, the rest single sightings kept as guesses.

Verified Tasks are pool allocated: every construction site draws memory from a pool with no size argument, then calls the constructor with its parameters. An early attempt to read sizes from nearby constants failed because those constants turned out to be constructor arguments, such as pause durations. All sizes are therefore lower bounds from observed fields, ranging from tiny flag tasks to path and animation tasks of a few hundred bytes.

Inferred The recommended rewrite order is the root and move interface first, then the simple-task base and scaffold, then trivial leaves, then the animation and pathfinding subtrees, with the NaturalMotion family last as the largest piece.

Unknown Three classes stay opaque: two keep all their own code in the encrypted range, and one intermediate base class has no virtual table in the recovered data at all, so its layout needs a recheck of its records.

What was decided or recommended

  • Accept the 99 task-type IDs and the slot map as the family's interface contract for rewrites.
  • Treat all sizes as lower bounds until task pool element sizes are measured.
  • Recover constructor signatures next, since argument values are visible at the pool call sites.
  • Defer the two encrypted classes and re-examine the base class missing its table before laying out its children.

How to reproduce it

Parse the executable headers and relocation table, join the batch class list with the RTTI virtual tables, and scan plain code for each table address as a relocated immediate to find constructors and destructors. Disassemble each method, track the object pointer through register copies, and record every field access with width and direction. Classify virtual slot targets by shape: constant stubs, getters, jump thunks, destructor fragments, or general code. Compare each slot against the base class tables to mark overrides, and aggregate field sightings across each class's own methods with confidence by sighting count.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first build double-added the image base to relocation entries and produced tens of thousands of bogus cross-references; the fix was one line. A sizing heuristic then mistook constructor arguments for allocation sizes until caller-window dumps showed several different values reaching the same constructor. About a quarter of the first constructor candidates turned out to be neighbouring functions or type checks rather than stores, and were reclassified. Tiny adjacent destructors share bytes, so their records needed filtering to each class's own table.

How to reproduce it

Scan the readable code for each class vtable address as an immediate, keeping only hits backed by a relocation entry; attribute each hit to its function via exported function bounds; disassemble with capstone; classify constructors versus destructors by whether the base call precedes the vtable store; confirm deleting destructors by the destroy, flag-test, pool-free shape; collect field offsets from object-pointer accesses in each class's own methods. Scripts and JSON data sit with the lane's scratch outputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first scan found almost nothing because of a relocation bug that added the image base twice; fixing it raised the hit count from 4 to over 500. A first classifier mistook branching constructors for deleting destructors until a real deleting destructor was read. The longest wrong turn was misreading deleting destructors as clone methods for about an hour; the call target is the plain destructor and the order is destroy-then-free, which settled it.

Class layouts: physics, collision, fragments and cloth

All 92 physics classes now have recovered object layouts and virtual interfaces: 89 virtual tables with 2,039 slots were classified slot by slot, constructors were found for 74 classes, 1,864 field evidences were harvested, and sizes were estimated for 88 classes. The headline patterns are a near-universal deleting destructor in slot zero, pure-virtual placeholders kept in the encrypted prefix, a strange slot aliasing trick in the bound family, and ten factory functions that build sibling classes together.

What was asked

Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the physics, collision, fragment and cloth class family: for each class say which virtual slots it overrides, inherits or introduces and what each function does in a phrase; find constructors and destructors by searching readable code for vtable stores; estimate object sizes from allocation sites or field extents; list fields with widths, kinds and confidence; record relationships; then describe the family tree, the shared base interfaces, the encrypted fraction and a rewrite order.

What was found

Verified Slot zero is the scalar deleting destructor in practically every table: 76 of 89 were confirmed by reading the function shape (flag test, vtable downgrade to the base table, free through the engine allocator, callee-cleaned return), 9 more match the shape closely, 2 are encrypted and 4 stay unknown. Slot one is usually not the vector deleting destructor here; only 8 classes show one, while 21 keep a pure placeholder and the rest hold ordinary virtuals.

Verified About a quarter of all slot entries point into the encrypted prefix, but they collapse to only 31 unique targets, most of them shared stubs. The most-used stub fills exactly the slots that derived classes override with real code, so it reads as the pure-virtual placeholder. Base interfaces that look heavily encrypted are really heavily pure; the meanings come from the readable overrides.

Verified The bound family aliases one virtual slot onto another through a tiny tail-call thunk: slot one re-dispatches to slot forty-eight through the object's own table, and thirteen of fifteen derived bound types inherit the thunk unchanged. The material manager does the same for two of its slots. The reason for the duplication is not known.

Verified Ten factory functions construct unrelated sibling classes: one builds the collision dispatcher together with all five narrow-phase algorithms, one builds capsule, sphere and surface bounds, one builds three broadphase strategies, three build the rope triple, two pair narrow-phase helpers with the manifold result, one initialises two fragment singletons, and one builds the three water classes.

Verified The fragment instance class shows textbook multiple inheritance: its constructors store the breakable-instance table, then their own table, then a second table at offset eighty for the streamable reference, and secondary-interface methods adjust the object pointer back by eighty.

What was decided or recommended

The recommended rewrite order is: the bound root contract first, then capsule, sphere, composite, polyhedron, box and the mesh chain; the instance chain with the fragment multiple inheritance; the self-contained collider; the joint contract with its three derived types; the broadphase strategies; the narrow phase validated against upstream Bullet headers; and finally archetypes, materials, rope, simulator, fragment managers and water, with the opaque allocator last. Field records carry high, medium or low confidence so later tools can weight them, and anything seen only once is marked a guess.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane analyzer script from the repository root with the project Python environment; it reads the game executable together with the RTTI tables, the function inventory and the call graph export, and rewrites the structures and statistics files in the lane scratch folder in about two minutes. It only disassembles the readable code range and keeps only vtable references backed by a relocation entry. Full per-class records, including every slot description, constructor, field and relationship, are in the lane data file.

What was confusing or went wrong

A script variable reused the name of the disassembly engine object and silently zeroed every result, because all detail accessors were wrapped in exception handlers; it took a full empty run to notice, and the fix was a rename. An early factory rule wrongly flagged constructors with inlined base-class initialisation as factories; the fix was to treat base-plus-derived stores as one constructor and only call unrelated sibling stores a factory. The slot-one findings were genuinely surprising: the expected vector deleting destructor is mostly absent, and the slot aliasing thunk has no confirmed explanation yet. Size estimation from allocation sites needed a field-extent cross-check before it could be trusted, and a few sizes remain suspect even now.

Class layouts: online service, session and leaderboard classes (rage::rl*, rage::sn*)

Verified The online family is 2,009 classes, of which 1,924 are four leaderboard templates stamped out 481 times each; the two workhorse templates share a single byte-identical virtual table across all copies, and every session task inherits an eleven-slot base interface whose table the earlier table recovery had missed.

What was asked

Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the online service, session and leaderboard classes: for each class the virtual table slot meanings, constructor and destructor behaviour, object size, field list with confidence, and relationships, plus a family tree, a shared-interface description, the encrypted-code fraction, and a rewrite order. Template copies were to be grouped, not analysed one by one.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into four leaderboard templates of 481 classes each plus 85 other classes. The leaderboard template carries a four-slot table identical in all copies: a deleting destructor, a getter returning the embedded info object, and a bounds-checked row accessor with a stride of 312 bytes. The leaderboard-info template has a seventeen-slot table that is different for every board but follows one pattern: a destructor, a per-board stub returning a schema descriptor pointer, shared getters in a handful of variants, and a stub returning a fixed constant. The leaderboard-update template has a three-slot table of plain field getters with no destructor at all.

Verified The session tasks share an eleven-slot base interface: destructor, a shared constant getter, two state methods touching a started flag and a state word, three opaque base slots, a per-task worker, a forwarder that calls the worker with a default argument, one more opaque slot, and a per-task stub returning a static descriptor pointer. Two tasks add a twelfth slot. The base table itself was found by reading raw memory after destructors kept storing an address no table list knew. Six fire-and-forget wrappers override nothing and add no fields.

Verified Session events form a two-slot hierarchy whose second slot is always inherited; most derived first slots just return a per-event static descriptor. Thirty-seven tiny descriptor classes have a single destructor slot each. Task objects are large, from roughly 160 bytes to roughly six thousand, while events with genuine constructors range from about a hundred to about six hundred bytes. About one slot target in five points into the encrypted first megabyte and could not be read; the base leaderboard tables and the notifier are fully opaque.

What was decided or recommended

  • Rewrite first the leaderboard trio, which is fully readable and identical across copies, then the task interface and tasks, then events; leave the encrypted base classes and the interface-only classes for later.
  • Treat all object sizes as lower bounds, not exact sizes; no allocation-site constants were recovered.
  • Parse the per-board schema descriptor blobs and the base task slot functions next; both are readable and were left untouched for lack of time.

How to reproduce it

Load the batch list and the recovered table list, scan the unencrypted code for each table address as a four-byte value using a sliding window, map each hit to its containing function with the function inventory, and disassemble the slot targets and the referencing functions. Shared slot targets are identified by counting matches across tables, and base tables are compared slot by slot for override status. The per-class records live in the structures data file with one entry per class.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first scan stepped through the code four bytes at a time and missed most constructor references, because immediate values are not aligned; only a byte-by-byte scan found them. Early field lists contained absurd offsets in the tens of kilobytes until three fixes landed: registers reused as scratch had to be untracked, functions building many objects had to be excluded from field evidence, and disassembly running past a tiny stub into the next function had to be cut off. One record initially suggested a leaderboard info class inherits from two bases at once; the slot evidence supports the interface half of that claim but the declaration half is still unresolved.

What was asked

Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the entity family: the entity, vehicle, ped, object and model-info classes. Verified Seven sizes are exact: the six model-info classes plus the vehicle base. How to reproduce it

Take the virtual table addresses from the RTTI recovery, search the unencrypted code section for each address as a four-byte value, and keep only matches confirmed by a relocation entry. Disassemble the containing functions, track the object pointer through register copies while discarding registers that get overwritten, and record every access through it with width and direction. What was confusing or went wrong

Two bugs wasted the first analysis pass: a register-name mapping that never matched, which silently produced zero fields for every class, and object-pointer tracking that never forgot, which attributed accesses through member pointers to the object itself and inflated some classes to four times their real size. Both were caught by comparing against the older-build sizes and fixed with stricter tracking. A planned size source, heap allocation sites, found nothing at all: none of these constructors are called directly from visible code, so all size evidence comes from strides, constructors and field touches instead.

Native handlers TASK_TIRED to WRITE_LOBBY_PREFERENCE: what they reveal

Ninety-four script-native handlers were disassembled and every one is now understood: most are thin wrappers that turn script handles into engine object pointers through shared pool lookups, while a few inline helpers, tail jumps and shared particle-effect unpackers cover the rest. The work produced proposed names for over eighty engine functions, twenty object fields, and several surprises, including natives that return values their documentation omits and one whose parameter the engine ignores.

What was asked

Disassemble the handlers of the ninety-four natives from TASK_TIRED to WRITE_LOBBY_PREFERENCE, recover the call-context layout, describe what each handler does at the engine level, and propose names for the engine functions and object fields they touch, with confidence levels.

What was found

Verified Every handler receives a single context pointer holding a return-slot pointer and an argument-array pointer; no handler checks an argument count. Handlers fall into five shapes: thin wrappers, tail jumps into context-taking engine functions, fully inline helpers, shared particle-effect unpackers, and one handler in the encrypted range that was skipped.

FindingDetail
Pool lookupsOne shared routine resolves all ped, vehicle and object handles; the pool is selected by a global pointer. Player indices go through a separate player-struct resolver.
Task idsEach task native funnels into one task-assign routine with a numeric task id; nine ids were recovered, and the two nearest-scenario variants share one id.
Particle effectsAll six trigger natives return a success flag the public docs omit, and take rotation angles in degrees that the engine converts to radians.
TimingThe wait natives accumulate either warped frame time, a fixed sixty-hertz step, or warped time that pauses with the game; the unwarped step is a hard-coded constant.
DeobfuscationThe string deobfuscator XORs with a four-byte repeating key into a static buffer, capped at sixty-four characters.
Ignored parameterThe ducking-toggle native reads two arguments but its engine function never looks at the second one; it always flips the current state.
Setters in disguiseThree natives with Can and Does names are actually setters of single flag bits.
Dead nativeThe lobby radio-HUD-on native shares its handler with forty-five others, including debug-only names, so it is almost certainly compiled to nothing.
Unused nativesNearly a third of the batch is never called by any shipped mission script.

What was decided or recommended

Proposed names were recorded for over eighty engine functions and twenty object fields with per-native evidence, so later lanes can confirm or correct them against decrypted code. The pool lookup, task allocator, particle spawn core and several network implementations sit in the encrypted first megabyte and need the decrypted view; the teleport native's fifth parameter cannot be resolved from shipped scripts and needs a live test.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone using section-aware address mapping, stopping at returns and unconditional jumps while keeping code reachable from forward branches; dump the first hundred or so instructions of each direct callee; read argument indices, boolean normalisation, by-value vector construction and return-slot writes from the instruction stream; and cross-check parameter lists against the public native database and call sites in the public decompiled mission scripts.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first extraction pass stopped at the first return instruction, which silently dropped code after conditional branches in the wait natives and bled neighbouring handlers into tail-jump stubs. Fixing the disassembler to respect branch targets and unconditional jumps changed several call attributions. Argument-index tracking also needed two iterations before register reuse stopped misclassifying reads. Both traps are worth knowing for the remaining native batches.

2026-10-03

Native handlers SET_CAR_PROOFS to SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_STANDING_STYLE: what they reveal

All 140 script natives in this batch follow one uniform design: each handler reads its arguments from a call context and forwards them to a single engine function, and almost all of those engine functions resolve the script handle to a game object through one shared lookup routine with separate pools for characters and vehicles.

What was asked

Disassemble the handler behind each of the 140 natives from SET_CAR_PROOFS to SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_STANDING_STYLE, work out the call context layout, describe what each handler does at the engine level, and propose names for the engine functions called and meanings for the object fields touched, using the public native documentation and the public decompiled mission scripts as the source of meaning.

What was found

Verified The call context carries a pointer to the argument array eight bytes in; every handler in the batch reads all of its arguments through it. Boolean arguments are normalised to zero or one and floats travel through vector registers, both with recognisable instruction idioms.

Verified Of 137 distinct handlers, 136 were disassembled and each calls exactly one engine function, all different. Four natives share one handler that sits in the encrypted part of the executable and was skipped.

Verified One shared lookup routine resolves script handles to object pointers for 114 of the 136 engine functions, taking a pool pointer plus a handle. The pool used splits exactly by native family: character natives use one pool, vehicle natives another. Two natives that take two handles look up twice, including one that consults both pools, which confirms the split.

Verified Character behaviour flags live in a run of flag words on the character object, with 47 single-bit assignments mapped to named natives and no two natives sharing a bit. Damage immunity flags sit at the same field with identical bits on both characters and vehicles, so that field belongs to a shared base class, with two relationship-based damage modes that actively clear each other.

Verified The nine decision-maker attribute setters share one code shape: convert the handle to an index, range-check it against 54 slots, lazily create a manager object, then write one field. Six attributes pack as bit ranges into one word and three are single bytes or bits, all mapped.

Verified All six coordinate setters route to one teleport function, differing only in flag constants. The money native sends its amount to a helper and sets only a flag bit inline. Health setting clamps to a maximum and consults the streaming system rather than storing blindly.

Inferred Handler argument counts match the public native database for every disassembled handler except two where the public entries list no parameters at all, so those two public entries look incomplete. About one native in seven is never called by the shipped mission scripts, mostly multiplayer or edge-case natives, but all still have real engine bodies.

Verified All but one shipped script share a single encrypted container version; the exception is an unencrypted leftover from an older container version that decodes with the same instruction set.

Inferred The most confusing source was an instruction-set document inside an otherwise reliable open-source tool repository: it describes a newer script target, not this game's, while the repository's code for this game's target is correct. The crate follows the code.

Tool that reads the encrypted code from the owner's running copy

The capture tool is built, self-tested, and ready: once the owner has the game sitting at its main menu, one command reads the decrypted code out of the running process, checks it against the file on disk, and writes the results to the private folders in about five seconds. Nothing leaves the machine, and the game itself is only ever read, never modified.

What was asked

The first megabyte of the game's code section is encrypted on disk and decrypted in memory at start-up by a wrapper library that ships with the game. The task was to write a small tool that reads that range back out of the owner's own running copy so it can be analysed like the rest, with strict limits: open the game read-only, never write to it, suspend it, inject into it, or attach a debugger, and write the outputs only under the private originals folder. A dry-run self-test against a small test program of our own had to prove the tool before it ever touches the game.

What was found

Verified The tool works end to end. Its self-test builds a tiny 32-bit test program, launches it, captures it through the same code path the game capture will use, checks the capture byte for byte, and terminates it. The code section matched the file exactly, including across a nonzero load-address shift, which proves the relocation-undoing step does its job on a live process.

Check Result
Synthetic relocation round-trip Pass, four load shifts including zero and overflow
Live code section vs file Exact match, zero unreadable pages
Live read-only data vs file Small differences, all in loader-resolved import tables, as expected
Loaded modules seen in test process Twelve, main module confirmed by two independent listings
Estimated full game capture time About five seconds for twenty-six megabytes

Verified The encrypted range shows zero standard function-entry patterns on disk, so any such patterns in the future capture will confirm readable code. Inferred The live capture is expected to take about five seconds, from timings measured on the file's own bytes and on timed memory reads. Unknown Whether the running game carries any run-time patches outside the encrypted range, and which helper libraries are loaded while it idles at the menu. Both questions are answered the moment the tool runs against the real game.

What was decided or recommended

  • A plain script on the project's existing Python setup was chosen over a compiled tool, because the cross-bitness memory reads it needs are supported by design and the self-test proves them on this machine. No new dependencies and nothing to build.
  • Differences outside the encrypted range are recorded as findings, never as failures: a mismatch there would mean the game or its wrapper patches code at run time, which is itself valuable to know.
  • The reconstructed executable the tool produces is for static analysis only and must never be launched, since the start-up wrapper would try to decrypt already-decrypted code.
  • Any future code that lists a 32-bit process's modules from a 64-bit tool must query both the toolhelp snapshot and the process-modules call with the 32-bit filter, or it will silently miss half the process. The first version of this tool did exactly that.
  • The capture outputs never leave the private folders and are never published; the public record carries only counts and conclusions.

How to reproduce it

Run the tool's self-test subcommand with the project Python from the repository root: it prints each stage and ends with a pass or fail line. A second script in the same folder replays the game-scale timing benchmark without needing the game. The lane folder also holds a run-book with the owner's steps, the coordinator's single command, and how to tell the live run worked.

What was confusing or went wrong

The module-listing gap was the real surprise: the first listing looked complete at seven modules, and only the absence of the most basic system library gave away that every 32-bit library was missing. It took a second enumeration call to see them. Less dramatically, the test program kept landing at the same shifted load address on repeated launches, so the retry loop built to catch varied shifts never saw variation; the synthetic round-trip covers that gap instead. The live game capture itself remains undone because the game was not running during this work and starting it was out of scope.

Rust reader: the RSC5 resource container

Verified The container that wraps nearly every binary game asset now has a clean Rust reader: header, size flags, decompression, the two memory segments, tagged pointers and the block-map slot. All 938 loose resource files in the game folder parse with zero failures.

What was asked

Write the foundation crate that asset-specific readers will build on: parse the resource header, decode the flags word into the virtual and physical segment sizes, decompress the payload, split it into segments, resolve the tagged pointers used for internal references, and read the block-map slot. Test against every loose resource file, and correct the public documentation where the files disagree with it.

What was found

  • Verified Every loose resource is one header plus a single compressed stream running exactly to end of file. The inflated size matches the size the flags word promises, to the byte, in all 938 files.
  • Verified Five asset types occur as loose files: web pages (most numerous), texture dictionaries, two effects package variants, and two drawable dictionaries. The ids match the values public tool sources list for those assets.
  • Verified Internal pointers use two tag values selecting the processor-side or data-side segment, with zero meaning null. Every pointer at a documented position in all 207 dictionaries resolves inside its segment, including every entry of every member list.
  • Verified The block-map slot is never populated in shipped files: dictionaries carry a reserved-but-empty slot, effects packages leave debug fill, and web-page resources are not rooted in the paged-object type at all. The engine evidently builds the map when loading.
  • Verified An earlier report of a truncated compressed stream in one effects package did not reproduce: the file inflates normally. The earlier failure was a short read in that probe script.
  • Verified No decryption is involved at this layer: loose resources are only compressed. The archive key belongs to the archive layer, which a parallel lane is handling.

What was decided or recommended

  • The crate rejects anything that does not inflate to exactly the promised size, caps inflated output well above the largest real file, and returns errors instead of panicking, so hostile input cannot crash or exhaust memory.
  • The block-map reader reports three honest states (absent, reserved-but-empty, populated) and exposes the raw words of any populated map it ever meets, since no shipped file has one to learn the entry layout from.
  • Next: run archived model, fragment, collision and navigation resources through the same reader once the archive lane delivers their bytes, and look there for a populated block map.

How to reproduce it

Build the crate and run its test suite; the integration test walks the game folder when the game directory environment variable is set and is skipped otherwise. What was confusing or went wrong

Two things cost time. First, the test compressor initially wrote a different stream header variant than the game uses, so every new unit test failed until the tests were pinned to the same variant. Second, a naive scan of every four-byte value for pointer-like tags drowns in false hits from floating-point numbers, hashes and texture bytes; only pointers at documented field positions mean anything, and the dictionary walk that checks those positions is the real validation.

What was asked

Write a clean Rust reader for the two archive containers the game ships, RPF and IMG version 3, covering headers, tables of contents including encryption, entry records, directories, and reading entry bytes. The reader had to be original work, platform independent, return errors instead of panicking, and prove itself by opening every archive in the game folder.

What was found

Verified The game ships two RPF versions: version 3 for the 45 audio banks and version 2 for the three model archives and the single game data archive. All tables of contents are encrypted, and one small data archive also encrypts its file contents.

Verified IMG archives are all version 3. All but four are encrypted; the four open ones are small path and script index files. Five archives are empty headers with no entries.

Verified Across all archives there are about three and a half thousand RPF files and fifty two thousand IMG entries. Roughly nine in ten IMG entries are engine resources in the RSC container, which uses standard zlib compression. No shipped RPF entry uses the archive-level compression flag.

Verified RPF version 3 stores name hashes instead of names, so file names must be resolved through an external hash table. Directory hashes in those archives do not resolve through public tables.

Inferred Three header words remain unknown: one in the RPF header that is always zero, one in RPF directory records, and one in the IMG header where a single file differs from all the rest. None affects reading.

The crate exposes one shared archive interface so later code can open either container the same way. The encryption key is located in the owner's game executable at run time by its published identifier and kept in memory only. The relocation table is fine; three lanes read it wrong

Earlier lanes disagreed about the executable's relocation table: one called it garbage, one found twenty thousand anomalous entries scattered through the code, one counted exact import matches, and one saw no entries at all in the encrypted region. A verified from-scratch parser shows the table itself is healthy, with just under two hundred ninety-two thousand entries that all check out, and each earlier disagreement traces to a concrete reading error, all now corrected.

What was asked

Settle the contradiction between four earlier lanes about the relocation table, produce the definitive relocation list and statistics, and map the whole code section page by page to find every encrypted or non-code pocket.

What was found

  • Verified The relocation table parses cleanly: only the two expected entry types appear, the bytes consumed match the directory size exactly, and every fixup site is backed by file content.
  • Verified The "garbage table" verdict was a scripting bug: the lane added the page address twice, scattering all sites to wrong locations. Re-running the bug reproduces its numbers digit for digit.
  • Verified All twenty thousand odd-looking entries sit inside the encrypted first megabyte, and their on-disk values are ciphertext, confirmed by uniformity tests. There are no scattered high-entropy pockets; an earlier lane misread its own location histogram.
  • Verified The encrypted region holds over twenty thousand fixup sites, not zero as reported; only their values are opaque, while their positions are exact and probably form the start-up stub's own fixup list.
  • Verified The import-table cross-check of about two thousand entries reproduces exactly, and a handful of references from code to the file headers are genuine.
  • Verified Page-by-page mapping finds no second encrypted region: two hundred fifty encrypted pages, sixteen pages of jump and pointer tables, and everything else code, including some zero-heavy initialisation code and tiny stub functions first mistaken for padding.
  • Verified Both function inventories contain entries inside ciphertext that must be excluded: several hundred in the new Ghidra export (which at least labels the region) and a few thousand in the lane estimate.

What was decided or recommended

The new relocation list replaces all earlier counts as the source of truth, with on-disk values inside the encrypted region marked as ciphertext. Downstream tools must drop ciphertext function entries from both inventories. The stub-fixup theory and the exact table seams inside mixed pages are left for a runtime lane and the function-inventory lane.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane scripts in order with the project Python: a boundary scan by page entropy, a manual relocation-directory walk cross-checked against the parsing library, a bug-reproduction script, uniformity tests on the odd values, and a per-page classifier combining entropy, pointer density and aligned fixup runs. Outputs are a compact relocation list and one record per code page.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two page-classification metrics failed before the third worked: plain linear disassembly misfires whenever a page starts mid-instruction, and resync disassembly then proved too permissive since nearly any bytes decode as something. Pointer density plus runs of consecutive aligned fixups turned out to be the reliable table signal. Separately, several dense initialisation pages first classified as tables or padding and were only corrected by reading their bytes.

All of the game's shaders can be extracted and translated to validated SPIR-V with free tools that now live in the project's tools folder. The game ships 102 shader programs in 6 graphics-card variants (612 files), all using shader model 3.0 bytecode inside a simple container. After removing duplicates there are 969 distinct shader programs. The recommended path is a small extractor, then the DXVK project's shader compiler to SPIR-V, then SPIRV-Cross to Metal shading language, with the official SPIR-V validator as the gate.

What was asked

Establish the game's shader container format from file headers and public documentation, count the shaders, and find, test and where allowed install the tools the project needs: an extractor for the container, disassemblers and translators for Direct3D 9 shader bytecode, and SPIR-V tools. Recommend a pipeline from the game's shader files to SPIR-V and to Metal shading language.

What was found

Verified The shader files sit as loose files in the game's shared shader folder, so no archive tool is needed for them. Each container starts with a four-character magic word, then a list of vertex-shader fragments, then pixel-shader fragments; every fragment carries its parameter names and a size-prefixed bytecode blob, followed by technique metadata. A purpose-written extractor parsed all 612 files with zero failures and every blob checked out as well-formed shader model 3.0 bytecode with full parameter tables.

Verified The six card-specific folders are mostly copies of each other: two are byte-identical, two more differ from the base set in only one or two files, and the remaining two carry cheaper variants of a few dozen shaders. Deduplication leaves 969 distinct programs out of 10,134 blobs.

What was decided or recommended

  • Use the SDK disassembler for inspection. Do not adopt the DirectX 11 decompiler.
  • Before translated shaders can run, not just validate, the renderer team must settle how shader resources and inputs are bound, because the translator's output follows DirectX 9 conventions the new renderer has to mirror.

Run the lane's extractor over the game's shader folder (read-only), which should report 612 files parsed and 969 distinct programs.   • The first batch test reported hundreds of MojoShader failures that turned out to be a bug in the test script's file mapping, not in the tool. After the fix all three language profiles passed everything.

Original functions can be executed for comparison, but not with Unicorn on this machine

The planned checker approach works, with a different engine than planned. The Unicorn CPU emulator crashes on every execution attempt on this machine, so the lane built a small 32-bit harness that runs original functions natively through the operating system's own compatibility layer instead. Fifty small functions were executed with hundreds of random inputs, most ran cleanly, and two trial Rust rewrites matched their originals on all 200 inputs each.

What was asked

Prove or disprove that original game functions can be executed outside the game for comparison testing of Rust rewrites. The plan named the Unicorn emulator: map the executable, set registers and stack inputs, run each function until it returns, and record the return value and memory effects. The lane was also asked to cover harder cases (calls between functions, global data, system imports, floating point, object methods), measure speed, and design what agreement between original and rewrite means.

What was found

Verified The emulator engine is unusable here. Every execution attempt crashes the whole process, including a minimal test of one trivial instruction with no hooks attached, and including non-x86 guest code. The fault is inside the emulator's own library, with a different crash code on different runs.

Verified A 32-bit helper program built with the project's Rust toolchain runs original functions correctly. It loads the executable's bytes with standard relocation fixups (a count cross-checked against an independent tool, matching exactly), calls one function at a time with chosen inputs, and reports registers, flags, floating-point state and changed memory as structured output. Faults are caught inside the process and reported with the failing location instead of crashing.

Verified The first of the code section's megabytes is encrypted or compressed on disk (entropy near the theoretical maximum, undecodable as instructions), while the remaining nine megabytes are normal code. Functions in the encrypted part cannot be executed from file bytes at all.

Verified Of 50 sampled small leaf functions run 8 times each, naive random inputs completed only about one run in eight, while shaped inputs (pointers aimed at scratch memory) completed over half, and a follow-up with better stack inputs brought 43 of 50 to fully passing. All failures were memory access faults, never illegal instructions. Repeated runs were bit-identical.

Verified Harder cases behave as needed: a real nested call between two game functions executed end to end; a global data read returned the correct startup value; an unresolved system import faulted deterministically at exactly the expected address, which is what makes it interceptable; legacy and modern floating-point instructions both work and their outputs are captured.

Verified Two hand-written Rust twins of original functions agreed with the originals on all 200 random inputs each, including calling-convention stack accounting on a stdcall function.

What was decided or recommended

The checker should use native 32-bit execution, not Unicorn, on this machine: one worker process owns the relocated original plus the linked rewrite, calls either side through the same trampoline, and compares return values, stack accounting, written memory, outgoing calls with arguments, and floating-point state. Bitwise floating-point equality should be the default, with per-function tolerance only where declared. Functions in the encrypted region and functions needing live operating-system state are out of scope for the checker and should be tracked as blocked rather than failed.

How to reproduce it

Build the scratch helper and twin crates for the 32-bit Windows target with the installed Rust toolchain (offline build, no extra dependencies), then run the driver scripts in the lane's scratch folder: one maps the executable and samples leaf functions with a disassembler, one runs each leaf with random and shaped inputs and records structured results, and one compares the two Rust twins against their originals over 200 seeded inputs. The design document in the same folder describes the contract, the input generation policy, and the per-case handling.

The first leaf scan produced nonsense instructions because it started inside the encrypted region; an entropy map showed the boundary clearly and the scan was restricted to readable code. The emulator failure looked at first like a harness bug and was only settled by a minimal one-instruction test with no hooks. The native harness then crashed in its own trampoline for several rounds: the fault addresses first suggested an emulation quirk, but disassembling the generated bytes plus an in-process fault handler proved it was an ordinary stack bookkeeping bug (the host stack pointer saved on the wrong side of two push instructions). Low memory also turned out to be unmappable in 32-bit processes on this host, which forced relocation support earlier than planned. Each of these cost time but left a checkable artifact in the scratch folder.

How fast an agent swarm went through phase 0, and what that does and does not say about the rest

In the first 33 minutes of phase 0, 37 agent lanes finished 545 lane-minutes of analysis and wrote about 104,000 words of findings: roughly sixteen times faster than one agent working through the same tasks in sequence. That speed is real, but it was measured on the kind of work that parallelises best. The rewrite itself has not been timed yet.

What was asked

The owner noticed the project was moving faster than expected and asked for an analysis, an estimate of when it could finish, and a note on what swarm working is like in practice.

What was measured

MeasureValueNote

Lanes finished in that time37, none failedEvery lane delivered its report, its data files and a devlog entry.
Time per laneMedian 13 minutes, shortest 7, longest 33Subsystem surveys were quickest at a median of 11 minutes. The longest lane overran because the tool it was told to use did not work and it had to build a replacement.
Parallel speed-up16 times545 lane-minutes of work in 33 minutes of wall-clock time, with between 16 and 28 lanes running at once.
Concurrency limit reachedNone yetUp to 38 lanes ran at once with no rate limiting from the model provider. Each lane used about 180 MB of memory; the laptop had 9 GB free at the peak.
Mistakes caught by a second lane3 in the first hourThe encrypted code range the coordinator missed, an emulator that crashes on this machine, and a disagreement about the relocation table that is still being settled.

Why it was fast

  • Verified The tasks were independent. Each lane read the same file and answered a different question, so no lane waited for another.
  • Verified Every lane got the same written contract: where it may write, what it must deliver, how to label evidence, and a progress log to keep. The coordinator did not have to explain anything twice.
  • Verified Publishing was automated behind a check. A script refuses any devlog fragment containing addresses, local paths, byte dumps or code, so the coordinator could integrate fifteen entries at a time without reading each line first.
  • Verified Overlap between lanes was useful, not wasteful. Lanes that measured the same thing a different way are what caught the three mistakes above.

What slowed it down or went wrong

  • Verified The coordinator is the bottleneck. Lanes finish faster than one coordinator can read their reports properly. In the first hour most lane reports were read only as fifteen-line summaries.
  • Verified Lanes cannot be corrected once they are running. When the encrypted code range was discovered, sixteen lanes had already started without knowing about it, and their numbers have to be checked afterwards.
  • Verified Pushing every commit separately broke the project site for several minutes. See the entry on site build collisions.
  • Verified Lanes disagree. Two independent function counts differ by about fourteen thousand, and two lanes describe the same relocation table as clean and as mostly garbage. A swarm produces contradictions at the same speed as findings, and each one costs a further lane to settle.
  • Inferred Quality varies with how much of a lane's evidence comes from running code against the real file. Lanes that measured were reliable; the one lane that worked mostly from forum posts was corrected within hours.

The estimate, and how much to trust each part

These are estimates made on the first evening, before any function has been rewritten through the full pipeline. The pilot in phase 2 replaces them with measurements.

0. MeasureFinished within a dayMeasured: most of it took an hour. One megabyte of code is encrypted on disk and can only be read once the owner has started the game.

2. Pilot1 to 2 daysMeasures functions per lane per hour and the false-accept rate. Every estimate below is a guess until this exists.

Rewrite2 to 5 weeksAssumes 30 lanes, each completing 4 to 10 small functions an hour around the clock. 82% of functions are under 256 bytes and about 13,000 are duplicates of one another, which favours the low end. Added up: a rewritten game that runs on its own with the original renderer in roughly 6 to 11 weeks, and a 64-bit build with a new renderer on three platforms in roughly 4 to 6 months. The first figure rests on one comparable project, the agent-driven Modern Warfare 2 decompilation, which took about ten weeks to become playable with fewer agents, fewer functions and the benefit of symbols.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep lanes independent and overlapping. Do not remove overlap to save tokens; it is the swarm's error correction.
  • Measure before estimating. The phase 2 pilot is short on purpose.
  • Move routine coordination, such as integrating finished lanes and posting status, onto cheaper models or scripts, and keep the coordinator for decisions and review.
  • Treat phase 0's speed as the ceiling for analysis work, not as a forecast for the rewrite.

How to reproduce it

Each lane's log records when the coordinator launched it and when it exited. Subtract the two for each lane, add up the durations, and divide by the wall-clock time between the first launch and the last exit.

Tools: building for the three target platforms

One Rust code base can already build and run for both Windows targets on the project machine, and macOS builds belong on macOS runners, not on this machine. A hello-world crate compiled for all three Windows targets and each binary ran. A macOS binary also linked locally through a cross-linker, but only a Mac can run, sign, or ship it.

What was asked

Work out how the project builds one Rust code base for Windows on x64, Windows on ARM64, and macOS on Apple silicon, from the project machine and from continuous integration. Test the local toolchain, try cross-compiling to macOS, and research runners and their cost, the Vulkan SDK and MoltenVK in CI, macOS signing, and how similar projects set up their builds.

What was found

Verified The local machine builds and runs all three Windows targets with no extra setup. The compiler ships native linkers for each one.

TargetBuildRun
Windows ARM64yesyes, native
Windows x64yesyes, emulated
Windows 32-bit x86yesyes, emulated

Verified Static linking of the C runtime removes the need for a redistributable install. The test binary then depends only on core system libraries.

Verified Cross-linking a macOS Apple silicon binary on Windows works for a trivial program using the Zig linker driven by cargo-zigbuild, with no Apple SDK installed. The output has the right Mach-O header for an ARM64 executable.

Inferred That cross-linked binary is a compile check, not a shippable build. Anything using macOS frameworks needs the real Apple SDK, whose licence restricts it to Apple hardware, and nothing here can run the result. Real macOS builds must happen on a Mac or a macOS CI runner.

Verified Standard CI runners are free with no minute cap for public repositories, so the three-platform build matrix costs nothing once the project is public. Suitable runners exist for each target, including an ARM64 Windows runner and current Apple silicon macOS runners.

Verified The Vulkan SDK is a free download and MoltenVK is permissively licensed, so neither needs buying. Both install in CI through maintained setup actions or direct downloads, and macOS runners can also install them from Homebrew.

Verified Ad-hoc signing is enough for development builds on macOS, but a clean first launch of a downloaded release needs paid developer membership, a distribution certificate, and submission to Apple's notarisation service, which is itself free.

Verified Three similar projects were read: a Sonic recompilation, an open game engine, and a GTA IV recompilation. All build each platform natively on its own runner, cache dependencies and compiler output, pin tool versions, sign macOS builds ad-hoc in CI with real signing reserved for releases, and ship Apple bundles as compressed tarballs rather than zip files.

What was decided or recommended

  • Build Windows targets locally and in CI with plain cargo; keep the C runtime statically linked so there is nothing to install.
  • Use the Zig-based cross-linker locally only as a macOS compile check, and do every real macOS build on a macOS runner.
  • Standardise CI on one runner per target, a pinned Rust toolchain with a shared build cache, a pinned Vulkan SDK installed by a setup action, and ad-hoc macOS signing, adding paid signing and notarisation only for tagged releases.
  • Organise the Rust code as one workspace with a crate per boundary: shared types, platform layer, renderer, engine subsystems, the 32-bit replacement library, the checker, and packaging tasks.

How to reproduce it

Install the missing Windows target with rustup, then build a hello-world crate for each of the three Windows targets and run each binary. Rebuild with the static C runtime flag and confirm the system library list shrinks. Install cargo-zigbuild, add the Apple silicon Rust target, and cross-link the same crate for macOS, then inspect the output header to confirm it is an ARM64 executable. The full commands, versions, hashes, and CI sketches are in the lane report.

The cross-linker first failed to find its own Zig binary because a system launcher stub shadowed the real interpreter; pointing it at the project interpreter fixed it. The first Zig download arrived truncated and had to be retried with hash verification. A system tool that locates compiler installs reported nothing even though the compilers work fine, which cost a short detour before plain builds proved the linkers were there all along.

Tools: reverse engineering helpers

Most of the helper tooling works on this machine, but two things failed plainly: neither demangler handles bare type names without a wrapping trick, and the bundled emulator crashes on every run. The project now has tested commands for diffing, listing, disassembling, parsing and demangling, and a clear note on what to avoid.

What was asked

Find, install and test the tools that complement the main disassembler for this project: an object differ, a relocatable-object exporter, shipped library-identification and similarity data, LLVM-style listing tools, two portable analysis suites, seven Rust crates for disassembly, parsing, hooking, emulation and demangling, plus the demangler in the installed build tools. Every tool had to be run on this machine, not assumed to work, and the demangling command had to be proven on twenty class names from the executable.

What was found

Verified The object differ runs natively and diffs 32-bit objects correctly, flagging a single changed constant with a near-total match score, but it refuses 64-bit ARM objects. The relocatable-object exporter ships an exact build for the installed disassembler version, confirmed from its manifest but not yet activated.

Verified The disassembler ships ready-made library fingerprints for five compiler generations in both 32- and 64-bit flavours, including the one matching the executable's linker generation, plus similarity-search scripts and weights. No queryable database exists yet; one must be built after analysis finishes.

Verified The installed build tools contain native listing and demangling programs but no LLVM listing tools. An official portable LLVM build for this processor exists (a large download) and was deliberately skipped.

Verified One portable analysis suite runs natively and reads the executable fully (machine type, section count, debug path, build date); the other runs emulated and agrees, additionally naming the linker generation. All Rust parsing and disassembly crates built and agreed with each other on headers, sections, imports and entry code.

Verified Both hooking crates refuse to build for the native processor and both build and run their tests for the 32-bit target the game uses, including an enable-and-disable hook round trip. The emulator package imports and maps memory but crashes hard on every emulation start in both 32- and 64-bit modes, so it is unusable here; its Rust twin shares the same engine core and licence and was not built.

Verified A scan found 1688 type names in the executable (1579 classes, 109 structs). Neither demangler reads a bare type name directly: one echoes it back or emits garbage, the other errors or keeps a prefix. Wrapping each name in the type-descriptor form before demangling fixed both engines, scoring twenty out of twenty on each, with matching results.

What was decided or recommended

  • Use the object differ for object-level comparisons, the build tools lister for headers and imports, and the native portable suite for second opinions.
  • Use the tested Rust crates for disassembly and executable parsing, and the tested demangling wrapper recipe in both Rust code and one-off commands.
  • Use the safe Rust hooking library for 32-bit targets with the C-based one as fallback, both fenced off from native builds.
  • Tag library code with the shipped fingerprints matching the executable's linker generation, and run similarity search against a local database once analysis lands.
  • Do not install the portable LLVM bundle, do not use the emulator on this host, and do not link copyleft-licensed emulation code into the project.

How to reproduce it

  1. Run the differ with two 32-bit objects, one symbol and dash for stdout; expect a structured diff naming the changed instruction.
  2. List the executable with the build tools lister and either portable suite; all three should report the same machine type, section count and import count.
  3. Build the small Rust test programs from pinned crate versions and run them against the executable; parsing results should match the listers exactly.
  4. Demangle twenty type names by stripping the leading dot, wrapping each name in the type-descriptor form, and running either demangler; expect a plain class line from each after removing the descriptor suffix.
  5. Build the hook tests for the 32-bit target and run them; expect the detour to reroute and then restore the call. Confirm the native build of the same tests fails.
  6. Start any emulation call in the bundled emulator package; expect the process to die without an error message.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Downloads silently landed outside the repository because a child shell did not inherit the working directory; the files were moved back and re-verified by hash. Future work should use absolute paths everywhere.

Verified The first disassembly test decoded from the wrong offset and produced nonsense; decoding from the real entry point produced a clean result. The first demangling tests also failed until the wrapping trick was found by trying the descriptor form directly.

Verified The emulator failure was silent: no exception and no output, only a dead process. Unbuffered step-by-step runs isolated the crash to the emulation start call itself.

How our code can get into the game

Our replacement functions can ride into the game as a proxy system library placed next to the executable, the same way community plugins already load, and nothing in the game's own checks looks at such a library or at patched code. The one thing that needs care is the start-up wrapper: the entry code loads a helper library from the game folder that prepares hidden start-up data before the real game begins, so our loader must wait until that finishes before touching anything.

What was asked

Work out, by research and static analysis only and without launching the game, how a project-built 32-bit library can be loaded into the running game and replace individual functions: which community mechanism to reuse, which libraries the game loads early enough to proxy, whether any integrity check would notice, and how the loader itself should be designed.

What was found

Verified The game statically imports three proxyable system libraries early enough to carry our loader, and none of them ships in the game folder, so a file placed next to the executable is picked up automatically. The community loader defaults to one of those names and recommends it in its readme; our loader should take a different one so both can coexist.

Verified Community plugins load inside library initialisation, before any game code runs. The community loader also has a deferred mode that waits for the game's first system call, but only other game titles use it; this game uses the default early path.

Verified The game's signature verification checks exactly one thing: the Rockstar Social Club library in the Program Files folder, confirmed as Take-Two signed. Save-game encryption uses the data-protection API and is unrelated. No code path was found that verifies the game executable itself, lists loaded modules for checking, or watches for patched bytes.

Verified The entry code resolves system functions by hand, loads a helper library from the game folder, calls into it in a retry loop, then invokes start-up callbacks that are all zeros in the file on disk (so the helper must fill them in at run time) before jumping to the real game code. The helper's imports show process and module inspection, memory reading, debugger checks, and the ability to end the process.

Verified The community fix project finds game code purely with named byte patterns (over a thousand collected, with per-version alternatives and no hardcoded addresses or version checks) and waits with watcher threads when code is not visible yet. Searched against our build, about half match exactly once and form named anchors; the rest belong to other game versions, plus a small set matching more than once that needs disambiguation.

FactValueWhat it means
Proxyable early importsThree system librariesOur loader can enter before any game code runs
Files the signature check verifiesOne: the Social Club libraryOur library and patched code are not covered by it
Named patterns collectedOver twelve hundredA large pool of candidate anchors
Patterns matching exactly onceAbout six hundredUsable anchors for the hook table
Helper library reaction to our codeNot known staticallyTop question for the first live run

What was decided or recommended

  • Build the loader as a project-owned proxy under the system library name the community loader does not use, with the small set of used functions forwarded to the real system copy; also support running as a community-loader plugin from the same codebase as a fallback.
  • Do almost nothing at load time; wait with an anchor-watching thread until game code is provably final, then install hooks, each behind an on/off switch driven by a start-up file and a local command channel, failing closed on any mismatch.
  • Use the pure-Rust detour library (permissive licence, native per-hook enable and disable) as the primary hook mechanism, small assembler adapters for class methods on the stable toolchain, direct slot writes for virtual tables, and mid-hooks only for observation.
  • Never touch the helper library's memory or threads, and assume it can see our module until a live run proves otherwise.

How to reproduce it

List the executable's import table with a PE parser and confirm which system libraries it resolves at load time and which files exist beside it in the game folder. Disassemble the few hundred bytes at the entry point and note the hand-rolled library loading, the helper-library calls, and the manual start-up callback invocation. Map every cross-reference to the signature and crypto imports and disassemble around each call site to see which file path is built and checked. Collect the community fix project's pattern strings, match each against the code section with wildcard support, and count exact, multiple, and zero matches.

What was confusing or went wrong

The start-up callbacks being all zeros in the file looked like missing data until the entry code's manual callback loop made clear they are filled in at run time. Two early readings of the entry code were wrong on first pass (how the helper name is encoded, and an address-range slip that briefly suggested odd export locations) and were corrected by re-parsing the bytes precisely rather than by hand. Web page fetches kept truncating, so both community projects were read as local copies in scratch instead, and only the pattern facts were kept. Most pattern variables in the community source share one generic name, so anchors are identified by file, line, and bytes rather than by a meaningful name.

Subsystem survey: physics and collision

The game's physics is RAGE-native collision code over a statically linked Bullet broadphase and narrow phase, with NaturalMotion Euphoria driving ragdolls, and no Havok anywhere. The survey counted 94 physics-owned classes, 792 related strings, and at least 789 physics functions in readable code, concentrated in one large engine block plus fragment, material, and entity-glue regions.

What was asked

Survey the physics and collision subsystem of the original executable by working directly on the file with Python: extract its classes from run-time type information with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, identify its operating system and library dependencies, compare against public knowledge, note frame-rate dependencies, and leave rewrite notes with a ranked list of what to understand first.

What was found

Verified The subsystem owns 94 classes: 19 collision bound types from boxes and spheres up to composite, mesh, and octree bounds; live instances, three collider types, joints, rope, constraints, archetypes, materials, a simulator, sleep management, a level world, broadphase variants, Bullet narrow-phase algorithms, and a fragment family for breakable objects. Sixteen more classes in other systems carry physics names, and 24 Euphoria behaviour classes plus two fragment render dictionaries sit at the boundary.

Verified Both the broadphase and the narrow phase are Bullet-derived, with Bullet class names appearing both under the engine namespace and without any namespace. Euphoria appears as behaviour, effector, and engine classes in a dedicated animation namespace, reached through dedicated physics instance types. No Havok class or string exists in the binary.

Verified Game entities attach through a single physics entity class with 72 virtual functions, the parent of pedestrians, vehicles, and objects, with matching network mirror classes. Fragments use multiple inheritance with the largest tables in the subsystem at 65 and 66 slots, while the simulator exposes only 8 virtual functions and the level world only one, so most of their interface is non-virtual.

Verified Of 792 related strings, the most revealing are resource paths for fragments and natural motion data, ragdoll state messages, task parameter asserts for ten Euphoria behaviours, debug dump formats for collision state and velocity, 19 wheel friction surface names, tuning keys for damage, inertia, and self collision, and broadphase debug text. Collision file extensions, Havok names, and physics source file paths are all absent.

Verified Relocation clustering plus virtual function targets attribute at least 789 functions and about 309 kilobytes of code to the subsystem across 168 clusters, with disassembly spot checks passing on 94 percent of sampled sites. About two-thirds of the attributed functions sit in one large engine block covering bounds, colliders, joints, rope, archetypes, both Bullet phases, and the simulator, with separate regions for fragments, materials, and game-side glue.

Verified The subsystem calls almost no operating system functions directly: only thread synchronisation primitives and a thread affinity query were found in its code. The C library is statically linked, file access goes through the resource system, and both Bullet and Euphoria are statically linked.

Inferred The physics stepper takes variable frame time as a parameter rather than using a fixed-step constant, since no frame constant is referenced from physics code. This matches public reports that running above 60 frames per second breaks vehicle handling, ragdolls, object physics, and helicopters, which community fixes address by restoring frame-rate scaling.

What was decided or recommended

A rewrite should proceed from bound primitives and mesh bounds with a bounds-file reader, through instances, broadphase, narrow phase, colliders, joints, the simulator, the level world, fragments, and game attachment, leaving the Euphoria bridge for last together with the animation work. Pure geometry queries, solver steps, and broadphase operations can be checked in a CPU emulator in isolation, while stepping, level queries, streaming, entity glue, and behaviours need the running game. Fixed-step-only simulation would be a behaviour change, so the rewrite must reproduce variable frame-time quirks, and field layouts, file formats, and the behaviour interface still need to come from debugger work or community sources.

How to reproduce it

Four scripts in the lane scratch folder run in order with the project Python environment: an environment check that verifies the encrypted prefix against its mirror section, a class scan that filters the shared type inventory and measures every virtual table through relocations, a string scan that filters the shared string inventory with physics patterns, and a cluster scan that groups code references with slot targets and spot-checks them with the disassembler. Each script reads only the original executable and the shared probe inventories and writes only to the scratch folder, finishing in about ten minutes. The class, string, and cluster data files it produces hold every address and count behind this entry.

What was confusing or went wrong

Several name filters misfired before review caught them: audio hardware voices, pixel-shader fragments, render phases, camera graph parameters, and a particle attribute all matched physics patterns and had to be excluded by hand, while one iterator class lost its enclosing scope to a name printer bug and had to be re-read from its mangled form. Tiny clusters pairing two type descriptors turned out to be data tables embedded in code rather than functions. A text search over the single-line string inventory hung and had to be replaced with a JSON load. Two Euphoria behaviour name strings looked like noise until the matching behaviour classes confirmed them, and the absence of collision file extensions was checked three ways before being trusted.

What was asked

Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools for the game's script files: decompilers, compilers and disassemblers. Establish where the scripts live, and the script file header and encryption used on PC. Clone the public decompiled-scripts repository as reference and report its coverage and most-used native functions. Finish with at least one script from our copy disassembled.

What was found

Verified Scripts ship inside two archives per episode (main and network), six archives in total, holding 940 scripts. The archives use a newer format than the classic one: only their directory is encrypted, while the script data itself sits raw, so scripts can be recovered by their headers alone.

Verified Every script on this PC build is encrypted but not compressed, with a versioned header carrying code, statics and globals counts. The decryption key is derived locally by the tool from the owner's own executable at run time; no key material was copied, printed or stored anywhere.

Verified The decompiled reference set holds 869 scripts and about 3.8 million lines across the three episodes, making 621,220 calls to 2,206 distinct native functions. The most called natives are injury and death checks, debug print helpers, the timer, and the wait call, which appears in 829 of 869 scripts. The reference predates our game build, so its counts differ by two scripts and its native names need re-mapping.

Carve scripts from the game archives by scanning for the script magic headers and validating their length fields. Count reference coverage by matching all-caps call names across the decompiled text files.

  • The tool rejected absolute file paths with a file-missing error; its inputs are patterns matched against the current folder, so it must run from the scripts folder.
  • The tool targets an older .NET version than the installed runtime, so every run needs a roll-forward setting.

Tools: the future Rust engine's libraries

A survey of Rust crates and C libraries for the future 64-bit engine found a maintained, permissively licensed crate for nearly every need, with three licence flags and one platform risk to resolve. Verified Seventy-three crates were checked against the package index, twenty-two repositories had their build configurations read, and every recommendation below names its version, licence and maintenance state as of the survey date.

What was asked

Find the best maintained Rust crate or C library with bindings for each need of the future engine: Vulkan bindings and allocators, Metal bindings, windowing and input, audio output and 3D audio, decoding, physics, maths, compression, archive parsing helpers, networking, scripting, profiling and the upscaler SDKs. Check which build for Windows on ARM64 by reading build configurations, flag every licence outside the permissive set, and end with a recommended dependency list. Research only; nothing was installed.

What was found

Most of the stack is uncontroversial. Vulkan goes through the long-standard binding whose repository is still active, with a pure Rust allocator beside it. Windowing and gamepad input collapse into a single C library that already supports Windows on ARM64 and Apple silicon. Audio output, the game mixer, physics, maths, compression, parsing helpers, networking and the profiler each have a maintained crate with recent releases. The 3D audio answer is the maintained wrapper around the now open source Steam audio SDK.

Four findings needed more care. First, only one crate in the survey tests Windows on ARM64 in its build configuration; everything else is trusted there because it is pure Rust on what is now a top-tier compiler target, while crates with C build steps each need one compile check. Second, the audio decoding library is pure Rust and complete but carries a weak copyleft licence that needs sign-off, and it cannot decode the game's videos, so a video library is still required for those. Third, the physics engine the original game derived from has only tiny or stale Rust bindings, so the maintained pure Rust physics engine wins despite the family resemblance. Fourth, upscaler bindings are new or placeholder, except for the Metal ones, so thin project-owned bindings are expected later.

Licence flags, all Verified from package metadata or primary sources:

  • Audio decoding: weak copyleft, file level. Usable inside a larger work but needs an explicit decision.
  • Video library: copyleft terms that depend on build options; a minimal build keeps obligations small but they still exist, and only this library decodes the game's videos.
  • OpenAL: rejected. Its Rust bindings are frozen since 2019, the maintained implementation is copyleft, and the system framework is deprecated on the Mac.
  • Upscaler and store SDKs: proprietary redistribution terms each; relevant only at the upscaling phase.

What was decided or recommended

Standardise on the table above. Prefer the single C windowing library over the three-crate windowing plus gamepad plus audio combination. Prefer the pure Rust allocator over the C++ one for the simpler ARM64 story. Take the maintained pure Rust physics engine and drop the idea that matching the original engine's physics family buys fidelity, since behaviour is rewritten rather than carried over. Write thin project-owned upscaler bindings at the upscaling phase instead of waiting for the ecosystem. The full versioned list with reasons, risks and rejected alternatives lives in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

  1. Query the package index API for each candidate crate and record version, licence, release date and download counts.
  2. Run package searches for the binding families where the crate name is uncertain (physics, spatial audio, video, networking) and confirm the maintained candidate by release date and repository activity.
  3. Read the build configuration files of each main repository and note which target triples and machine types are tested.
  4. Read the platform tables in the audio, windowing and physics project readmes, and the licence files of the profiler, the spatial audio SDK and the video library.
  5. Compare against the existing upscaling reference for the upscaler SDK state rather than re-researching it.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two searches returned misleading names. Verified A crate named exactly for the physics engine turned out to be an unrelated virtual machine project, and the crate named for the game's video format is a reserved-name stub; both wasted one lookup each before the package descriptions gave them away. Build configuration scanning missed several projects that use non-standard workflow filenames, which was corrected by listing one project's workflow directory directly. The oldest Vulkan binding release looked stale until the commit history showed active maintenance without recent releases, a reminder that release date alone misleads. Several platform claims rest on consistent secondary sources rather than primary documents because the time budget did not stretch to reading every upstream manual; those are marked as inferred in the report.
