Tools: archives and compression

Every game archive now opens: all 49 package files and all 254 disc images list cleanly with a scripted tool, and the one build quirk found along the way, an encrypted sidecar file nobody had flagged, decrypts with the same method as everything else.

What was asked

Establish which container and compression formats this build uses from file headers, then find, test and where allowed install the tools to list and unpack them, and prove the pipeline by extracting samples.

What was found

Verified The build uses two package-file versions: the audio banks use the newer one and the player-model archives plus one small data archive use the older one. Nearly all disc images are encrypted; four small ones are stored open. All loose resources share one container version and are zlib compressed. No lossless-console compression appears anywhere in this PC build, and no package entry uses the format's own compression flag.

  • Package files list 3,522 contained files; disc images list 52,718 entries, with zero failures in either set.
  • Audio bank entries carry content hashes instead of names; a public hash table resolves 99 percent of them to readable names.
  • Scripts ship only inside archives: 941 compiled scripts across eight archives, none as loose files.
  • The small data archive was the surprise: unlike every other package file, its file content is encrypted as well as its table, and it decrypts to a readable text file.

Verified Tool results: the Rust archive crate builds but cannot open this build's encrypted tables, so it is not usable alone. The Python audio-bank library resolves names and extracts correctly for audio banks but misreads model archives. The classic C# archive browser was evaluated from its source only; it supports this exact game version but needs a desktop install. The zlib libraries in both languages inflate identical bytes.

What was decided or recommended

  • Scripted work should use the lane's small independent reader plus the Python crypto library: it is the only tested path covering all archive kinds, compression and the encrypted sidecar.
  • Audio-bank names should come from the MIT-licensed hash table behind a quiet wrapper.
  • Rust code should use the standard zlib crate; the LZX crate is recorded for console reference work only.
  • The desktop archive browsers stay owner-installed tools for interactive browsing, not part of the pipeline.

How to reproduce it

Verified Run the lane's listing script from the repository scratch area: it loads the archive key from the owner's executable into memory, validates it by trial decryption without ever displaying or storing it, then lists every archive into a JSON file and extracts a handful of small samples into the asset cache. The Rust check builds a scratch project against the archive crate and the compression crates and inflates one loose texture dictionary three ways for identical output.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Two naming traps cost time. The audio-bank name table looks empty at first because its entries are hashes, not broken offsets; comparing against the Python library's hash table confirmed the bytes match. The script-archive samples also came from an episode archive at first because its folder path ends the same way as the base path; per-archive counts in the report use exact matches. A first Rust attempt failed on a wrong argument type for the LZX crate and a bad relative path; both were fixed by reading the crate source and using an absolute path.

Subsystem survey: vehicles

Vehicle code is scattered across the executable rather than living in one module, with about one hundred thirty RTTI classes, six drivable vehicle types, and handling data held in plain structs with no RTTI at all. Helicopters and planes turn out to be subclasses of the automobile class, all network replication code for vehicles sits in the encrypted part of the file, and the shipped data files match binary format strings exactly, which gives the rewrite free parser tests.

What was asked

Survey the vehicle subsystem of the original executable by static analysis only: extract its RTTI classes with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, list its operating system and library dependencies, summarise public knowledge, note frame-rate dependencies, and write rewrite notes with a ranked list of what to understand first.

What was found

Verified The class tree is small and single-inherited: a base vehicle class with six descendants (automobile, bike, boat, heli, plane, train), plus a vehicle model info class, a factory, a scanner, task info, two network events, a paint shader effect, wheel render data, and two audio entities. Helicopters and planes derive from the automobile class, and the multiplayer mirror classes repeat the same shape.

Verified Handling, wheel, suspension, transmission, chassis, and siren classes do not exist in RTTI. Their behaviour is reachable through strings instead: six suspension position names, three transmission position names, per-wheel suspension health formats, force-transmission script tunables, wheel friction surface names, and a thirty-seven-field handling file with one hundred seventy-eight entries.

Verified One thousand fifty-nine code references cluster into one hundred fifty fine groups and fifty-two broader regions spanning the readable code, holding roughly eight hundred virtual methods as a firm lower bound and an estimated one to three thousand functions in total. The largest regions are vehicle and police audio, car driving and door tasks, drive-by flags with seat and door logic, damage audio, and the get-in and get-out task family.

Verified Vehicle code makes essentially no direct operating system calls; its dependencies are internal engine systems (physics, fragments, audio, rendering, tasks, networking, streaming). Third-party markers found are Bullet broadphase collision, zlib, Bink video, and NaturalMotion animation. Havok, PhysX, FMOD, Granny, SpeedTree, and Scaleform markers are absent.

Verified Six loose data files were read: handling data, vehicle definitions, car colours (hot-reloadable according to its own header), car groups per city district, vehicle extras with boat boarding points, and train camera nodes. A boat boarding-points format string in the binary matches the extras file line for line.

Verified Public bug reports tie vehicle behaviour to frame rate: acceleration and top speed change above ninety frames per second, helicopters and cameras misbehave past sixty, and the standard advice is to cap at sixty or thirty. The binary holds frame-lock settings, slow-motion effect names, and time-scale strings, but no explicit per-frame vehicle constants were found.

An early function-estimate lane had concluded the code section was unreadable on disk, but per-window entropy and disassembly showed clean code after the encrypted first megabyte, so the survey proceeded on the readable remainder. Subsystem survey: networking

The executable still contains the complete multiplayer stack even though this edition removed multiplayer: entity replication, session management, presence and clan services, leaderboards, voice message types, and socket, HTTP and TLS transport. Games for Windows Live is gone without a trace, and the backend points at Rockstar Online Services instead. About half of the game replication layer appears to sit in the encrypted part of the code section, so it cannot be studied statically.

What was asked

Survey the networking subsystem from the executable alone: the classes, strings, code locations, operating system dependencies, public knowledge, timing behaviour, and rewrite notes, with a ranked list of what to understand first.

What was found

  • Verified Class names recovered through run-time type information show two layers: a game replication layer with per-entity-type sync wrappers, sync parsers, several dozen network event types, replicated task types, interpolation helpers, and array replication for pickups, player info and script variables; and an online services layer with session tasks, session events, wire message types, and a live-services manager with a Steam backend.
  • Verified Leaderboards dominate the class count: nearly fifteen hundred template bindings covering several hundred multiplayer mode schemas across ranked and standard boards for races, episodic content, team, competitive and co-operative modes.
  • Verified No reference to the old PC online platform remains anywhere: not in strings, class names, or imports. The replacement backend is named throughout: presence, party, invite, clan and sign-in events, matchmaking and clan web service endpoints, and Rockstar service hosts for auth, online services and cloud.
  • Verified Transport is raw sockets plus the engine's own HTTP client and statically linked TLS. Most socket imports are referenced from readable code in a select-loop client pattern with no listening sockets; all crypto imports are used for certificate checks and protected session-id storage.
  • Inferred The game replication layer and socket startup live mostly in the encrypted code region: most of its class tables and all of its diagnostic strings have no references from readable code. Session, presence, HTTP, stats upload and leaderboard code is in the readable region, in on the order of two dozen code areas totalling roughly a quarter of a megabyte.
  • Inferred Voice chat is a leftover surface only: message types, menu tokens and error text exist, but no voice transport was found, and the similarly named audio engine classes are unrelated sound synthesis voices.

What was decided or recommended

A rewrite should start with the pure serialisation pieces (bit buffers, message framing and ids, sync data layouts), then session state machines against a fake transport, and leave sockets, NAT traversal and the defunct server endpoints for last with loopback harnesses. The next step for this subsystem is to prove whether any network code is still reachable from the menus, and to recover sync data layouts from the readable parser code.

How to reproduce it

Parse the executable headers for sections, imports and relocations; scan read-only data for run-time type descriptors and validate complete object locators and class hierarchies against the relocation table; extract printable strings and filter by network keywords; resolve every relocation in the unencrypted code and keep targets matching network class tables, strings or socket and crypto import slots; group nearby hits into clusters; spot-check samples with a disassembler used only as a verifier.

Find the script engine's native function table using byte patterns published by the open-source script debugger scrDbg, enumerate every registered native as a hash plus handler pair, confirm the name-hashing function, and name as many natives as possible against public name lists.

What was found

Verified Registration takes two shapes that both reach the same table insert routine: a small group carries its own failure check per native, while the large group calls through a shared wrapper that holds the check once. The table routines match the published open-table design entry for entry, including the probing rule and the empty-slot markers.

Verified Native name strings are absent from the executable, so scripts and the engine meet only through hash values. Seven cases where the two public databases disagreed on a hash were settled against the registered values: three favour one database, one was a misattributed name, and three turned out to be genuine alias pairs where both hashes are registered.

Inferred Roughly the first megabyte of the code section reads as high-entropy bytes rather than code, so it is likely decrypted by the start-up stub at load. Only the shared debug handler points into that region; everything else registered sits in readable code.

What was decided or recommended

  • The enumerated hash-to-handler list is the ground truth for this build's natives; later work should consume it rather than re-derive it.
  • The new name-hash algorithm stays open. The recommended next step is to extract the hashes that compiled game scripts actually call and attack the algorithm from those pairs, using the two-halves bit structure as the main constraint.
  • Handler code clusters into a few regions, which should make per-subsystem handler mapping straightforward.

How to reproduce it

  1. Search the executable's code for each published scrDbg pattern with wildcard bytes; each should occur once, pointing at the script-engine data.
  2. Read the table insert routine next to the table anchor and note its two-argument shape and probing loop.
  3. Find every push of a known native hash immediate followed by a call to the insert routine or its wrapper; pair each hash with the handler address pushed just before it.
  4. Match the collected hashes against the public SCO-Toolbox and HappinessMP lists to attach names, and hash the old list with the Jenkins function to confirm the old generation.

What was confusing or went wrong

Each hash in the small registration group appeared twice, which first looked like dual registration into two tables; disassembly showed the second push belongs to a failure-logging path, not a second table. The new hashes first appeared to have two bits structurally clear, which sent the analysis down a blind alley of masked and split-hash theories; the full-bit entries in the same list turned out to be old-hash placeholders, but the true new hashes really do keep those bits clear and the algorithm still resisted some sixty candidates plus seed-inversion, suffix, modulus and shift-family attacks. The shared debug handler points into the encrypted code region, so its runtime behaviour could not be checked statically.

What was asked

The owner reported that the published site did not seem to be working. The pages returned normally when checked a few minutes later, so what had happened?

What was found

  • Verified The coordinator had just started integrating lane results one commit at a time, pushing after each. Twelve commits went up within about a minute.
  • Verified The build history shows each push starting its own site build, and every build except the last of a burst ending immediately with "Page build failed". Only the final push of each burst produced a working site.
  • Inferred A build that is still running is cancelled or rejected when a newer push arrives, and it is reported as a failure, not as superseded. While a burst is in progress the site can serve an old version or fail to load.
  • Inferred Each failed build probably also sends the repository owner a notification.

What was decided or recommended

  • Commits stay one change each, but a batch of commits is pushed once, after the last one. The agent rules and the commit tooling now do this.
  • The status tick makes at most two pushes: one for the batch of integrated lane results and one for the progress files.
  • After a batch, check that the newest build reports "built" before telling anyone the site is updated.

List the repository's Pages builds through the GitHub API and compare their creation times, statuses and durations with the times of the pushes.

Verified A working asset pipeline for models, textures and map placement now runs on the project machine: a community map extractor built from source converts game map archives to open glTF models and standard texture files, and the long-standing archive browser SparkIV runs for day-to-day inspection.

What was asked

Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools the project needs for drawable, fragment, texture dictionary, collision, animation and map placement formats, test each one on this machine, collect the best public format documentation, and recommend which tool to standardise on for each job.

What was found

Verified Nine candidates were examined. Three were installed and tested successfully:

  • SparkIV, the archive browser and viewer for game archives, models and textures. The latest prebuilt release launches and stays running on this machine.
  • A community map extractor plus its pinned game-asset parsing library. It compiled with no errors and converted a small map sector (62 archive entries) into 41 out of 41 models with textures, with nothing skipped.
  • A Rust parsing crate for a newer game in the series. All 108 of its self-contained tests pass here. It cannot read this game's files directly, but its structure is the best template for a new loader.

Verified Four more were collected as reference but could not be fully tested: a Blender add-on whose code needs Blender itself (not installed), a maintained SparkIV source fork (the prebuilt release covers the need), and two recompilation-project resource readers, one without a licence statement and one under a restricted licence, so both are read-only references.

Verified The public wiki documents several formats field by field (drawables, collision dictionaries, placements, and the two text map formats), but the texture dictionary and vehicle fragment pages are stubs with no layouts; the parsing library source fills that gap.

What was decided or recommended

Inferred The project should standardise on SparkIV for browsing archives, the extractor plus parsing library as the asset pipeline, and a new clean-room Rust loader modelled on the Rust crate's design using the documented layouts. The closed-source editor OpenIV, the 3ds Max plugins, a paid modelling tool and Blender itself are left for the owner to install.

How to reproduce it

  1. Fetch the latest SparkIV prebuilt release from the project's own release page, unpack it into the tools folder, and launch the browser.
  2. Clone the map extractor and the pinned asset library revision, build the extractor with the installed .NET SDK, and run it against a copy-safe output folder with framework roll-forward enabled.
  3. Clone the Rust parsing crate and run its test suite with the Rust toolchain; no game files are needed.
  4. Read the public wiki pages for the drawable, collision, placement and text formats, and the parsing library source for the texture and fragment layouts.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified One named Blender add-on repository no longer exists on its hosting site, so it could not be evaluated. One candidate name in the task turned out to be a different game series' recompilation project, not a texture tool; its resource reader was still useful as documentation. A first extraction test silently used an archive with no matching map files and produced nothing; re-running against a real map sector worked. The main closed-source editor's website showed an expired certificate on the day, so its details were confirmed from secondary sources instead.

Tools: audio and video

The project now has a tested open toolchain for all of the game's sound and video: FFmpeg reads every cutscene video, vgmstream reads the game's audio banks, and a small Python library extracts those banks from the archives. All sampled game audio turned out to be a single simple codec, which makes the port's audio job smaller than expected.

What was asked

Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools the project needs for audio and video: the game's audio containers and codecs, speech and radio streams, Bink video files, and user music. Test whether vgmstream supports this game's PC audio, install a portable FFmpeg build and use it to identify the Bink files without converting them, identify the audio container format from headers, and name the Rust crates that could decode each format in the port.

What was found

Verified The game ships nine Bink version 1 videos: two long TV channels for the base game, four shorter ones for the two episodes, and three small clips. FFmpeg's Bink support reads all nine, reporting resolutions from 256 by 192 to 512 by 384 at about 30 frames per second, with Bink DCT audio at 22050 Hz (one small clip uses 11000 Hz mono; two clips have no sound).

Verified All game audio lives in encrypted RPF version 3 archives: forty in the base game plus three per episode. The entries inside are Rockstar AUD banks holding between one and over a hundred streams each. Every sampled bank, across ringtones, ambient radio, a music station and speech, uses IMA 4-bit ADPCM at 24000 to 32000 Hz. No MP3, Vorbis, XMA or Miles audio was found in the PC game audio path.

Verified vgmstream supports this game's PC audio: it reported correct metadata for all five sampled banks and decoded one stream to WAV. FFmpeg cannot open the AUD banks at all, so the two tools complement each other rather than overlap.

Inferred User music works by scanning a user music folder for WMA and MP3 files, and a small encoder program beside the game exports replay clips to Windows Media Video 9. Both conclusions come from program text strings, not from running the game. Unknown The exact folder path on a player's machine was not checked.

What was decided or recommended

The project should standardise on FFmpeg for video and Windows Media formats, vgmstream for inspecting and decoding game audio banks, and pyrpfiv for scripted archive extraction. The closed-source OpenIV editor is left as an optional install for the owner; nothing in this phase depends on it.

For the port itself, the lowest-risk path is the Symphonia crate family (MPL-2.0, pure Rust) for the ADPCM game audio and MP3 user tracks, plus a project-written AUD container reader, with FFmpeg bindings covering Bink video and the WMA edge case. There is no maintained pure-Rust Bink or WMA decoder, and the one Bink-aware Rust framework found is under the AGPL and therefore excluded.

How to reproduce it

Install a portable FFmpeg build from one of the Windows build sets linked on the FFmpeg download page, the command-line build from the vgmstream releases page, and pyrpfiv from PyPI. Point FFmpeg's probe tool at the game's movie files, extract audio banks from the sound archives with pyrpfiv using the owner's own game executable, and run vgmstream in metadata mode on the extracted banks. Full commands, versions and checksums are in the lane report.

What was confusing or went wrong

The extraction library's documentation names older game versions, but it parsed the current version's archives without complaint, so the version list is out of date rather than the code being broken. The same library prints thousands of log lines and fills in its file list through a side channel instead of returning it, which needed a small wrapper. The word ivaud, the community's name for the PC audio format, appears nowhere in the game executable, which briefly suggested the format might be absent until vgmstream identified the banks directly.

Subsystem survey: world, entities and object pools

The entity hierarchy survived intact in the executable's type data, but the world container, the pools and the population manager left no type traces at all, which means they are almost certainly static code with sizes baked in as plain numbers. Map data on disk uses text definition files plus binary placement files, and the public placement format matched the bytes on disk.

What was asked

Survey the world, entities and object pools subsystem working directly on the executable file: list its classes with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, note its operating system dependencies, check public documentation, note frame-rate dependencies, and rank what to understand first.

What was found

Verified The run-time type data holds thousands of classes, of which about two dozen belong to this subsystem. The entity tree runs from a common root through dynamic and physical entities down to objects, buildings, dummy placeholders, interior and portal instances, with seven model definition classes and a set of world query helpers.

Verified No trace of a world container, pool collection, population manager, file loader or placement class exists anywhere in the type data or the strings, so these are most likely static classes with no virtual tables. Pool sizes appear nowhere as text and must be plain numeric constants in code.

Verified Useful strings include pool exhaustion errors, population manager startup and shutdown messages, portal and room tracking text, placement provenance wording, level-of-detail distance settings, and pickup save and load errors. Map files on disk come in per-district triplets of definition, archive and binary placement files, and the placement header matches the public format documentation.

Verified Code references to this subsystem are scattered across the whole program by link-time code generation, with the densest spots around model definitions with portal tracking and around generic objects. About sixty direct references group into eighteen small clusters totalling tens of kilobytes, with a lower-bound estimate of roughly two hundred functions. Entity code itself calls no operating system functions directly; timing and threading calls live in neighbouring code.

What was decided or recommended

  • Start the rewrite with the model definition table and the text definition parser, then binary placement loading, then the pool allocator, then the world grid and scanners, then pickups, portals, population and detail policy.
  • Parsers, pool allocation sequences and handle encoding can be checked in a CPU emulator in isolation; streaming interplay, render equivalence and population timing need the running game.
  • Public format documentation for placement files is confirmed and can be relied on; pool capacities and the world grid layout are undocumented anywhere and are the highest-value unknowns.

How to reproduce it

Parse the executable's type descriptors, object locators and virtual tables from its data sections, extract printable strings, and join the relocation table against those targets, keeping only reference sites in the unencrypted part of the code section. Cluster nearby sites, validate standard function prologues with a disassembler, and curate out audio, interface, task, camera and network classes before clustering. Scripts and data files are kept with the survey.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first clustering attempt produced hundreds of meaningless clusters because audio, interface and task class names share the same substrings; only curation first made the picture usable. The encrypted first megabyte of the code section contains no relocation entries at all, so this method is blind there and the world and pool code may sit in that hole. One vehicle class slipped through a name filter and was caught on review.

Subsystem survey: streaming and resources

The streaming subsystem splits into a readable edge and an opaque core: 49 related classes were identified through type information, but the central file-device and archive code has all of its virtual methods in the encrypted part of the executable, while the media readers, one loader variant and the resource-dictionary plumbing are readable.

What was asked

Survey how the game loads assets at run time: the streaming request system, resource files and pointer fix-up, archives, file devices, asset dictionaries and memory budgets. The work was done by direct analysis of the executable file with Python, without the pending Ghidra analysis and without decrypting or running anything.

What was found

  • Verified 49 classes belong to this subsystem, 47 with measurable virtual tables totalling 597 slots. The file layer is a virtual filesystem family of 8 device classes with 34 to 38 virtual methods each: local disk, memory buffer, relative path remount, network stream, growable buffer, caching decorator, archive files and a streaming device.
  • Verified the pageable resource system centres on a small base class with 8 typed dictionary instantiations covering animations, textures, drawables, physics bounds, particles and render mesh fragments, plus typed cross-file references that are resolved at load time.
  • Verified the main streaming scheduler classes have no type information at all: no descriptors exist for the streaming controller, the streaming module, the asset stores, or archive and resource manager classes, so they must be static classes or plain structures and can only be found through strings and code references.
  • Verified every virtual method of all 8 file-device classes and all parameter-stream classes points into the encrypted region, as do nearly all asset-loader methods. Readable code covers the media stream readers, the direct loader variant, dictionary plumbing and file-system call sites.
  • Verified 533 distinct subsystem strings, revealing a slot-based request model with active and requested state, per-area streaming set files, an on-disk cache with validation and a defragmentation pass, virtual paths split between shared and platform-specific data, streamed fonts, and a heavily duplicated resource-validation failure message in five languages.
  • Verified about ten code regions attributed to streaming through 492 specific references plus 73 direct file-system calls, all sample-checked as genuine code. They cover dictionaries, archives, async streaming, low-level file access, caching and cross-file references.
  • Verified compression uses a statically linked zlib, movie playback uses Bink and Windows Media components, and audio streaming uses DirectSound plus the multimedia timers.
  • Inferred the readable streaming code is on the order of low hundreds of functions; the encrypted region holds most of the archive and scheduler method bodies, so no exact total can be measured from the file on disk.

What was decided or recommended

Rewrite work should start with the readable and documented parts in this order: local file device and virtual paths, archive reader checked against public format notes, decompression, resource block loading with pointer fix-up, dictionary containers, cross-file references, then the cache and the request scheduler last, since the scheduler needs dynamic analysis or a decrypted image. The archive format and the general resource design are publicly documented, but the streaming set files, the cache format, the defragmentation pass and the scheduling and eviction policy are not and remain the unknowns.

How to reproduce it

Parse the executable headers and relocation table, scan the data sections for C++ type descriptors and object locators, resolve base classes through the hierarchy descriptors, measure virtual tables by counting consecutive relocated code pointers, filter class names for streaming and resource keywords, filter the string table to trustworthy sections only, and collect relocation fixups in the unencrypted code that target subsystem tables, strings and file-system imports, then group nearby references into clusters and validate a sample by disassembly.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two traps cost time. First, a case-insensitive name filter matched unrelated classes such as camera script instructions and destroy-car tasks, and a word-boundary pattern silently missed the whole file-device family; both were caught by inspecting the candidate list and the filter was rewritten case-sensitively. Second, clustering code by synchronisation calls produced bogus mega-clusters because every subsystem uses locks; synchronisation was excluded from attribution and the clusters were recomputed from subsystem-specific references only. Public sources were thinner than expected: the archive format page is thorough, but the canonical modding SDK repository and the resource-format notes could not be located in the time available and stay open leads.

Script host and client variable replication plus a host-variables verification event account for 80 virtual functions whose code sits entirely in the encrypted region. Verified The interpreter announces itself through ten adjacent messages: unknown opcode, missing native command, unknown script name, three thread-reset diagnostics covering argument size, static variables versus stack size, and program identity, plus thread kill, array overrun, and clean exit notes. How to reproduce it

Run the lane scripts in order with the project Python environment: layout and candidate scan, hierarchy and full virtual-table scan, string filtering with independent raw-byte term checks, relocation-based clustering with spot disassembly checks restricted to the unencrypted range, message-neighbourhood and import-reference scan, then curation into class, cluster, and string data files. Every script asserts the unencrypted-only rule before disassembling anything. The relocation table, the runtime type records, and the credible-section string pool are the only inputs.

What was confusing or went wrong

The substring scr matches screen, describe, and discrete, and mission matches transmission, so the first candidate list was mostly noise and needed two curation passes. The prior lane string inventory mixes garbage decoded from encrypted bytes with real strings, so only three sections were trusted. About three of forty spot disassemblies decoded to implausible instructions where the sample landed mid-instruction, which was treated as sampling noise rather than evidence. The short tokens sitting inside the interpreter message block and the single throw message next to them could not be identified and are recorded as unknown rather than guessed at. Open format references and one engine-documentation set were left unchecked for lack of time.

A stock system demangler returned type names unchanged, so a purpose-built approximate decoder was written instead; it handles every name with zero failures.

  • The first register-argument measurement counted register saves as argument passing and overstated the result. Excluding save and restore instructions fixed it and the corrected numbers still support the optimisation finding.

The executable's data is now mapped: read-only data holds imports, over three thousand validated virtual tables, string and float pools; the writable area is mostly an eleven megabyte zero-initialised region with a few very heavily referenced globals; and the binary contains no C++ exception tables at all, which means later lanes never have to model C++ unwinding.

What was asked

What was found

Verified The nine sections do not overlap. The code section is about eleven megabytes and the read-only data section about two megabytes. Writable data is thirteen megabytes in memory but barely over one megabyte on disk, so most of it is zero-initialised. The small entry-point stub section is writable and executable, and the one megabyte blob beside it is uniformly maximum-entropy, so encrypted or compressed.

Verified Zero functions use C++ exception unwinding: no exception tables exist anywhere in the image, and only plain system exception imports are present. The build was most likely compiled with C++ exceptions disabled.

How to reproduce it

All analysis ran directly on the executable file with small Python scripts using a PE parser and a disassembler library, without starting the game. The scripts parse section headers, directories, resources and relocations, scan for runtime type structures and exception records with pointer validation, and cross-check every structure against relocation references. The first type-information scan found nothing, because the type descriptors live in writable data rather than read-only data, which is not the usual compiler layout. The version-information library call also failed and had to be replaced with a manual parse. What remains unknown is why the descriptors sit in writable memory and what restores the high-entropy pockets in the code section, if anything does.

What was asked

Verified There is exactly one thread-creation call in the readable code, and it follows a fixed sequence: create suspended, set normal priority, disable priority boost, resume. Locking is pervasive, with several hundred critical-section calls, and the synchronisation set is era-typical: critical sections, mutexes, semaphores, events and interlocked operations, with no newer primitives imported.

Verified Referencing analysis shows the render-thread name, the frame-timing log strings, the surviving command-line switches and several timer imports are referenced only from the encrypted region. Startup proceeds through numbered checkpoints with fatal exits after reading the command line once.

Inferred Public bug reports and mod fixes agree the simulation step is coupled to frame rate: vehicle handling, ragdolls, rotors, ladders and several interface speeds all change above console frame rates, so the rewrite's time step must reproduce the original arithmetic, not just the wall time.

What was found

Verified The executable imports a single graphics function and loads no shader compiler library, so every shader is precompiled and all drawing goes through graphics interface calls.

Verified The geometry buffer has four targets, lit by a dedicated deferred lighting shader with about thirty light parameters, with stencil masking for light volumes.

Verified Shadows combine a cascade atlas in two depth formats with cube shadow maps for point lights and a separate shadow conversion pass.

Verified The post chain includes exposure adaptation, bloom, depth of field, motion blur, light shafts and tone mapping, fed by quarter-size and blur scratch targets.

Verified The game folder holds just over one hundred unique shaders in six graphics-vendor variants, plus small text preset files, text vertex declarations, and an ordered preload list. Every shader is vertex and pixel shader model 3, nothing older.

Verified Class names show resource wrappers for textures, render targets and buffers, a dozen model and shader classes, twenty five render phases, thirty five small draw-command classes, and bucket-sorted draw lists built on worker threads.

Pointer tables: the functions calls alone cannot reach

Most of the game's indirectly called functions are now mapped: about three thousand virtual tables confirmed through type data, two dozen dispatch tables dominated by online-service handlers, over two thousand switch jump tables, and nearly fourteen thousand code targets that no direct call reaches. The planned method failed first — the relocation table turned out to be unusable — and the first pages of the code section are encrypted, so everything below comes from value-based scanning of the readable parts only.

What was asked

Find the function pointer tables in the executable's data, because functions reachable only through pointers are easy for analysis tools to miss. The task named five classes to look for: C++ virtual tables, C runtime initialiser arrays, callback and dispatch tables, switch jump tables, and anything unclassified, plus counts, the functions reachable only through pointers, the static constructor count, and the largest dispatch tables with string evidence.

What was found

Verified The relocation table cannot be used as a detector. Of roughly 292,000 entries, nearly half sit at unaligned offsets a linker would never emit, and under 3% of the values they point at land anywhere inside the image. Detection was rebuilt on values instead: runs of consecutive words in data sections whose contents fall inside the code section.

Verified The first 250 pages of the code section are encrypted or obfuscated: per-page entropy near maximum and no decodable instructions, against normal code entropy everywhere after a page-exact boundary. A separate section holds a byte-identical copy of that encrypted prefix plus one page. Table slots landing in the encrypted region, about sixteen hundred of them, have unknown reachability.

Verified Raw value scanning found over eleven thousand runs, but three fifths were text, not pointers: lowercase prose and UTF-16 strings fall numerically inside the huge code range all the time. A byte-pattern filter removed nearly seven thousand text runs, including every large fake dispatch-looking and fake initialiser-looking run.

Verified The confirmed virtual tables name just over three thousand distinct classes, mostly engine and audio names. Verified Nearly fourteen thousand distinct readable-code targets appear in data tables but in no direct call instruction; all but a small fraction also appear in no direct jump. These are the functions reachable only through pointers, as an upper bound, since calls from the encrypted region are invisible. There are zero TLS callbacks. What was decided or recommended

  • Later tools must not trust the relocation table for pointer detection; the lane's value-based tables ship as JSON instead.
  • Backup copies (the encrypted code duplicate and the twinned jump tables) should be deduplicated by content hash before any function counting.
  • The small unclassified runs still mix string fragments with real pointer pairs and need per-item review, starting with the ones flanked by encrypted-region pointers.
  • Static constructors stay unknown until an unpacking or dynamic lane reads the startup code; candidate groups are listed in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

Work only on a copy of the executable with read-only scripts. Map the sections and confirm the encrypted prefix by per-page entropy, then scan the file-backed data sections for runs of consecutive aligned words valued inside the code range. Drop runs whose bytes are UTF-16 or printable ASCII, confirm virtual tables through the type-descriptor name behind each table's header pointer, census direct calls by scanning readable code for call and jump opcodes, and verify jump-table encoding by comparing each nearby table-jump instruction's embedded address against the table address. The lane's scripts run in this order: layout survey, relocation probe, encryption probe, value scan, bridged and filtered passes, then relabelling.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first full analysis trusted the relocation table and reported sixteen tables; the real count was thousands. That failure took one probe to diagnose and forced the value-based rewrite. The value scan then reported over eleven thousand runs, most of them strings, and the classifier initially labelled nearly three hundred string runs as initialiser tables — the byte-pattern text filter fixed that but certainly left string fragments among the small unknowns. Two self-checks were built on flawed reasoning and caught before shipping: a span comparison meant to test address encoding is translation-invariant and proves nothing, and a merge pass for split runs was unnecessary because runs already spanned encrypted-region slots. Both were replaced with direct evidence.

Verified A TLS stack is linked in, identified by a large table of cipher-suite names and error strings plus a bundled set of CA certificates. Inferred The string set matches CyaSSL 2.x, the library later renamed to wolfSSL, circa 2012 to 2014. The start-up stub: a tiny loader, an encrypted first megabyte, and an external unlocker

The game does not start in its own code. A loader stub of about six hundred bytes runs first, loads a Rockstar wrapper module shipped beside the game, lets it prepare the process, then hands control to the normal C start-up routine. The first megabyte of the code section is encrypted on disk and a read-only section holds an identical backup copy of it.

What was asked

Explain what happens between process start and the game's real entry point: what the stub in the small executable section does step by step, what the one megabyte high-entropy section is, what runs before the real entry point, how the shipped launcher starts the game, and whether any of this interferes with analysis or with loading extra code into the process.

What was found

  • Verified The entry point sits at the first byte of a tiny writable and executable section. The stub finds the system library through the process loader list instead of using imports, then loads a wrapper module by name and resolves two single-letter functions from it by walking its export table by hand.
  • Verified The stub calls the first wrapper function once with no arguments, then calls the second one in a loop until it reports success, passing it the locations of the thread-storage and relocation tables. It then unloads the wrapper and jumps to the real entry point.
  • Verified The one megabyte section is byte-for-byte identical to the first megabyte of the code section, and that first megabyte is encrypted: maximum entropy, incompressible, and disassembles as nonsense. The boundary between encrypted and normal code falls exactly on a page boundary one page before the end of the copy.
  • Verified The encrypted region holds heavily used code: tens of thousands of call sites and over sixteen thousand linker-confirmed pointers from the rest of the program reach into it, including the call to the main window function from the C start-up code. It must be decrypted before the game can run.
  • Verified No game code references the backup copy. It is mapped read-only, so the game cannot corrupt it. It is most likely the wrapper's pristine reference for decrypting and integrity checks.
  • Verified Nothing runs before the stub except the operating system loader. The thread-storage callback list is empty, and the stub's own callback-dispatch code can never execute because its guard condition is always false.
  • Verified The real entry point is an ordinary C start-up routine of the expected compiler generation: cookie check, exception-handler setup, a check of the program's own headers, command-line retrieval, then a call into the main window function.
  • Verified The wrapper module exports only the two functions the stub calls. Its own code is obfuscated, and its imports show it can scan processes and modules, change memory protection, read process memory, terminate processes, and detect debuggers.
  • Verified Signature-checking functions are called from one cluster of game code far from the stub. The code verifies an Authenticode signature, treats a missing or bad signature as not verified rather than fatal, and inspects the signer certificate and timestamps. A separate pair of data-protection calls sits elsewhere and looks like save-data encryption.
  • Verified The game is normally started through a 64-bit launcher stub that reads two metadata files, supports store-specific launch paths with documented command-line flags, enforces a single instance, and hands off to the Rockstar Games Launcher, which starts the game itself.

What was decided or recommended

  • Inferred Static analysis of the first megabyte of code is blocked until it is decrypted; disassemblers will show garbage there, while callers elsewhere in the program stay visible. The import table is intact, so API usage remains readable.
  • Inferred Loading an extra module into the process is not blocked by the stub itself, but the wrapper scans the process before the game starts, so injected modules may be noticed. This needs live testing to confirm.
  • Inferred Replacing functions in memory at run time is mechanically normal, but the pristine backup copy and the wrapper's memory-reading ability mean integrity re-checks are plausible. Whether any run after start-up is unknown.
  • Inferred The wrapper's retry loop and the signature checks deserve dynamic observation in a sandbox before any lane depends on start-up behaviour.

How to reproduce it

All results come from static reads of the game executable and the two files shipped beside it, using a PE parser and a disassembler library from throwaway scripts. The checks were: section table and entropy survey; full disassembly of the stub section with manual decoding of its five embedded strings; byte comparison of the backup section against the code section; a page-by-page entropy scan to find the encryption boundary; counting linker relocation records that point into the encrypted range; reading the thread-storage directory and its empty callback list; disassembly of the real entry point; import-table review of the wrapper and launcher; and string and metadata review of the launcher. No game code was executed and no protection was defeated.

What was confusing or went wrong

Linear disassembly of the stub initially misread its embedded strings as instructions, which hid the real control flow until a raw dump revealed the call-and-capture pattern. A first scan for references to the backup section returned dozens of hits that all turned out to be misaligned decoding artefacts and coincidental numbers in graphics data, which only became clear after checking each one against aligned disassembly and the relocation table. The wrapper takes the thread-storage and relocation locations as arguments for reasons that remain unknown.

Collect public class and structure names for this game's engine from other builds and projects so they can later be matched to our executable: the RAGE API notes and investigation documents in LibertyRecomp, the IV-SDK headers, IV-SDK .NET, the IV multiplayer client headers, plugin-sdk GTA IV headers, and GTAV-Classes. Then extract the class names from our own executable, cross-reference the two sets, rank the 100 most important classes, and record every source licence. Names and layouts only, no code copying.

What was found

Verified Our executable names 3723 distinct RTTI types, demangled into 1664 distinct class names, of which 478 sit in the rage namespace. The largest families are tasks, cameras, network messages, animation, events, audio, physics, rendering commands, and particles.

Finding Count Meaning

Verified The core entity, physics, streaming, model info, camera, task, event, network and render-command names match across sources and our build, including all thirteen named render-command subclasses from the LibertyRecomp investigation. Two independent public readings of the player-info layout agree field for field.

Verified Four sources are GPL licensed (LibertyRecomp, IV-SDK, IV-SDK .NET, IV multiplayer), plugin-sdk is permissively licensed, and GTAV-Classes has no licence and no content: it was emptied by its owner and archived, so the rage primitives came from plugin-sdk and LibertyRecomp instead.

Inferred Several SDK struct names with a temporary air about them have no footprint in our build and are probably invented by SDK authors rather than real engine names; they remain useful as layout hypotheses but not as vocabulary.

Unknown A handful of engine classes the public headers describe as central, including the audio engine, graphics device, script program, and page streamer, have no type entry at all in our build. They may be renamed here, built without type info, or described from a different version.

What was decided or recommended

  • Every layout from an older build stays marked as unverified here until re-measured against our build, since IV-SDK itself warns that classes differ between versions.
  • Where two public sources disagree on a layout, both readings are recorded and neither is trusted; the next lane re-measures rather than picking a winner.
  • After the entity core, the highest-value documentation targets are the thirty top-100 classes with type entries here but no public documentation anywhere, mostly physics, rendering, audio, and task classes.

How to reproduce it

Scan the executable for the standard MSVC runtime type descriptor string prefixes, keep the terminated names, and demangle the simple and template cases; then fetch the listed public headers and documents as plain web pages and match unqualified class names, mapping the multiplayer client's mirror prefix to the game prefix. The lane's scratch folder holds the scan script, the raw name inventory, the public class data, and the cross-reference with the ranked hundred.

What was confusing or went wrong

Large public files arrived cut off partway, so three big headers and two long documents are only partially collected; the gaps are listed in the lane report for a follow-up with full-file fetching. Two guessed header paths returned not-found, which corrected the inventory rather than costing much: vehicle subclasses have almost no public PC layout, and the player-info mirror lives under a different filename than expected. The most confusing result was the missing type entries for supposedly central engine classes; absence of a type entry proves nothing for types without virtual functions, but for virtual-heavy classes it is a genuine puzzle left open for a string and vtable hunt.

2026-10-03

Correction: the first megabyte of the code is encrypted

About 9% of the code section is encrypted on disk, and the first look at the executable missed it. The first 1,028,096 bytes of the code section are indistinguishable from random data, and a separate section named .tbm holds a byte-for-byte copy of the same bytes. The remaining 9.9 MB is ordinary compiled code.

What was asked

A lane estimating the number of functions reported that the code section looked encrypted, which contradicted the coordinator's earlier reading. Which was right?

What was found

  • Verified Measured in 256 KB windows, the first four windows of the code section have an entropy of 8.00, 8.00, 8.00 and 7.97 bits per byte. Every window after that is between 5.6 and 6.6, which is normal for compiled code.
  • Verified The first four windows contain no standard function prologues and no padding between functions. Every later window contains hundreds to thousands of each.
  • Verified The .tbm section is exactly 1,028,096 bytes and is identical to the first 1,028,096 bytes of the code section.
  • Inferred The start-up stub in .rkstr probably decrypts this range in memory before the game runs, as part of Rockstar's protection for this build. A lane is analysing the stub; this has not been confirmed.
  • Unknown What code lives in the encrypted range, how many functions it holds, and why the same bytes are stored twice.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • The coordinator computed one entropy figure for the whole section, got 6.71, and wrote "not packed or encrypted". An average over 10.95 MB cannot show a 1 MB anomaly. The fix is to measure in windows, always.
  • The mistake was caught within minutes because an independent lane measured the same thing a different way. Two lanes looking at the same file from different angles is worth the duplication.
  • The Ghidra analysis had already started and was disassembling the encrypted bytes as if they were code, producing nonsense functions and call targets. It was stopped and restarted with that range split into its own block and marked non-executable.

What was decided or recommended

  • Until the range has been read from a running copy, every tool treats it as opaque data. It is excluded from function counts, from the queue and from the code map, and the progress figures state its size separately so the percentages are honest.
  • The coordinator first wrote that the project would never read this range from the running game, citing the anti-piracy rule. That was the coordinator's own over-reach, and the owner corrected it the same day: the anti-piracy rule is about piracy, not about analysing a copy the owner bought. The range will be read from the owner's own running, purchased copy and analysed like the rest of the code.
  • What is read that way is game code. It stays in the private, ignored folders and is never committed or published, like all other game code.
  • The project still distributes no game files, keys or cracks, and does nothing to help anyone run the game without buying it.

How to reproduce it

Read the code section with pefile, cut it into 256 KB windows and compute the Shannon entropy of each. Count the byte sequence of the standard function prologue and runs of padding bytes per window. Compare the first megabyte of the code section with the contents of .tbm.

Ghidra refuses project folders that start with a dot

Ghidra will not create or open a project if any folder in the project's path has a name starting with a dot. This repository keeps all generated files under a folder named .artifacts, so the first headless analysis failed immediately.

What was found

  • Verified Ghidra 12.1.4 headless aborts with "Path element starting with '.' is not permitted" when the project location is under a dot-prefixed folder. The check is on the path text, not on where the data physically lives.
  • Verified Script folders passed with the script path argument may live under a dot-prefixed folder. Only the project location is checked.

What was decided or recommended

The Ghidra project is addressed through a directory junction whose path has no dot, tools/ghidra-db, which points at .artifacts/cache/ghidra. The data stays with the other caches and Ghidra sees a path it accepts. Any lane that needs a Ghidra project must use the junction path.

How to reproduce it

Run the headless analyser with a project directory under any folder whose name begins with a dot.

2026-10-03

Why the route is direct to Rust

Lanes read decompiler output from a private folder and write Rust directly, with no committed C++ stage. Each rewrite is checked by running the original function and the Rust version in a CPU emulator from the same state. This follows from the owner's rule that no decompiled code may be committed, and from the goal that the game becomes 64-bit and portable.

The route changed three times

  1. Verified A from-scratch engine that loads the original assets. Rejected once the evidence showed that decompiling is fast and carries mission logic, AI and ragdoll behaviour across intact.
  2. Verified Decompile to C++, rebuild, then port to Rust. Rejected because only structures, symbols and Rust rewrites may be committed, so a C++ stage cannot be kept, and an uncommitted months-long intermediate is a loss risk.
  3. Verified Rewrite directly to Rust. Current route, and one phase shorter.

What the direct route costs

  • Verified Byte-matching against the original compiler is impossible for Rust, so every byte-matching tool in the reviewed projects is out. The check is an emulator comparison: results, memory writes and outgoing calls must agree. Both sides run in the emulator, so it does not depend on the game running on this ARM64 machine.
  • Verified The second check swaps accepted functions into the running game through an injected 32-bit DLL with a per-function switch. A regression is found by switching replacements off in halves.
  • Verified Known weakness: floating-point results can differ in the last bits, so those comparisons need a tolerance, and a tolerance can hide a real difference. The in-game switch is the backstop.
  • Unknown Whether the emulator comparison works at scale. It is our own design and no other project has proven it. The phase 1 gate of 50 accepted functions tests it.

Why Rust, and what that forces

Verified The Rust port exists to make the game 64-bit and portable to Windows x64, Windows ARM64 and macOS. That forces the following work, which is why 64-bit and renderer work wait until after phase 4.

  • Euphoria, the animation and ragdoll middleware, is statically linked 32-bit code with no source. It must be rewritten like game code.
  • Bink video needs a replacement decoder.
  • Resource files hold 32-bit pointers, so a converting loader is needed.
  • The script virtual machine needs pointer handles.
  • All Windows and Direct3D 9 calls go behind a platform layer.
  • The renderer must output motion vectors, depth and jitter for upscalers.
  • Inferred Path tracing on macOS would need native Metal, because MoltenVK does not expose ray tracing as far as we know.

Xbox 360 static recompilation against function-by-function rewriting

Inferred Lane D compared the routes. Its facts about the 360 projects come from their repositories (XenonRecomp, LibertyRecomp RAGE API). Its PC column is its own assessment. It concluded that the 360 route is the better base for a quick playable port and the worse base for reconstructing source.

Dimension Xbox 360 recompilation PC rewrite
Output Unreadable by design. Every function takes a machine-state context. The product is the readable code. No second lifting phase.
Rust suitability Hostile. Big-endian memory, reversed vector lanes and goto control flow would carry into Rust. Clean. Only names and layouts come from the 360 side.
Memory model Byte swap on every load and store, permanently. Little-endian 32-bit x86, like for like with modern hosts.
Time to playable Fastest demonstrated. One independent port reached gameplay except collision. Slowest. Playable only after a critical mass of rewrites.
New gameplay Constrained. Patches wrap original functions and the engine stays a black box. Unconstrained, at the cost of understanding everything.

Harness design taken from other projects

Thief 3 (MSVC 7.1, x86) has the closest toolchain and the most developed agent harness, so the plan copies its structure. The parts that make a compiler reproduce original bytes do not apply, because Rust cannot. The byte-match gate is replaced by the emulator comparison.

Parts taken, with the real numbers

  • Verified Queue. A script orders functions easiest first and lanes do not choose. Thief 3 scores instruction count plus 3 per branch, 2 per call, 10 per switch, 10 per exception frame and 1 per x87 instruction (next.py). Snowboard Kids 2 later fitted its weights by logistic regression, and stack size predicted nothing (blog).
  • Verified Claims. One file per claimed function, created atomically, expiring after 2 hours and renewed by every attempt.
  • Verified Context packet: the target, resolved references with names, structures touched, the most similar accepted functions with source, names that accepted callers already use, the family, and the best earlier attempt on a second pass (context.py).
  • Verified Attempt budget: cap of 12 per claim, stop after 4 counted attempts with no new best. The code comment cites replayed ledgers: 3 would have refused 10 of 1,219 matches to save 36 attempts, and 4 refuses 2 to save 18 (common.py). Inferred Another lane read the workflow document and recorded 3, so sources disagree. The code is more likely current. Snowboard Kids 2 reportedly gives up after about 30 attempts, seen only in a fork.
  • Verified Deferral is a normal outcome, recorded with a blocker tag. Permanently unworkable functions move to an exclusion list.
  • Verified Routing by size. Functions up to 31 bytes: 20 per worker, cap 5. From 32 to 79 bytes: by class, cap 8. From 80 bytes: the stronger model, cap 10. A second pass uses the other model. Workers stay under about 100 tool calls and up to 20 run at once.
  • Verified Families. Functions identical after masking references are grouped. One accepted member is stamped onto the rest and passed through the same gate with no model call.
  • Verified Guard rails live in tooling. Thief 3 workers write only under a scratch folder and run only four scripts, enforced by a pre-tool hook that also denies git (guard-settings.json).
  • Verified A lint runs on every candidate, and every batch ends with a sweep that releases stale claims and appends cost, attempts and deferral reasons to a ledger.
  • Verified Smaller ideas. Nigel defines a lane as a candidate command, a prompt template, and verify, success and reset commands (README). The asmlift prompt demands two deliverables of equal standing: merged work and a tool defect log ranked by cost.

Replacing functions inside the running game

The proven method in the GTA family is to build the rewritten functions as a DLL, load it through an ASI loader (a proxy DLL that loads plugin files at startup), and redirect each original function to its replacement with a switch per function. gta-reversed does this for San Andreas at 8,000 functions. Our second check has the same shape, with Rust in place of C++.

How gta-reversed registers and switches functions

  • Verified Registration contract: each class has a static function that registers its hooks, one central function calls them all, every function is installed with its address, and a function not yet reversed is marked so that it still calls the original (HookRegistration.md).
  • Verified Two-way hooks. Each hook can be switched between original and reversed at runtime, locked, restored to its previous state and written to a JSON file, and hooks are grouped by path (HookCategoryItem.cpp). An in-game debug menu toggles them.
  • Inferred Virtual functions are installed through a per-class macro taking the original virtual table address and slot count. The source is one pull request snippet whose body would not load.
  • Verified Layout assertions. Every reversed structure carries compile-time checks of its size and member offsets, so a wrong layout fails the build (Base.h). IV-SDK and the plugin-sdk GTA IV headers do the same.
  • Verified The injected build needs the exact expected executable bytes. A wrong build crashes randomly (gta-reversed-modern).

How those projects verified

  • Verified There is no test suite. A fork's instructions say testing is injecting the DLL and checking behaviour in the game. The layout assertions and the runtime switch are the whole mechanism.
  • Inferred re3 began in 2018 as single-function replacement by DLL to test reversed collision and physics inside the original game, and went standalone around April 2020. Search snippets only, because the original repository is gone.
  • This is why the emulator comparison exists. It catches what in-game playing misses, and it runs without the game.

Hooking notes

  • Verified MinHook 1.3.4 supports x86 and x64. safetyhook is C++23 for Windows x86 and x86_64. retour is a Rust fork of the detour crate: static_detour needs nightly, thiscall support needs rustc 1.73 or later, and its CI covers the 32-bit Windows target (retour).
  • Inferred A hook for a thiscall method (the C++ convention that passes this in ECX) is written in the fastcall shape with a dummy parameter for EDX. Three practitioner sources agree.
  • Verified Rust's 32-bit Windows target built a DLL exporting an extern "thiscall" function. Current Rust requires #[unsafe(no_mangle)].
  • Verified GTA IV needs the 32-bit ASI loader installed as dinput8.dll (setup notes). FusionFix finds code by wildcard byte patterns and installs mid-function hooks (example), but old patterns still fail on new builds, as the next entry shows.
  • Inferred To record a function's inputs and outputs from the real game, Frida's Interceptor is the standard tool. x32dbg has conditional tracing commands (index).
  • Unknown No guide to hooking by virtual-table slot was found.

Script engine and resource formats

  • Verified A game script thread is the base thread plus a 24-byte program name and flags. scrDbg and IV:MP agree on the offsets. Natives sit in an open-addressing hash table keyed by name hash. Threads run on an instruction budget. Globals are not paged, unlike GTA V. scrDbg finds all of it on the Complete Edition with ten byte patterns (scrDbg).
  • Verified The compiled script format has a 24-byte header, 79 opcodes plus push, and encrypted variants (SCO). Compiling with the wrong per-version natives mode silently mistranslates every native call.
  • Verified Resource files are literal memory images. Pointers are a 28-bit offset plus a 4-bit block type across a virtual and a physical segment, fixed up at load. Three independent sources agree. This is why a 64-bit build needs a converting loader. Structures inside a file can be identified by the virtual table values the resource compiler wrote.
  • Verified Archives: RPF2 for the main game, RPF3 for audio, IMG3 for streaming. An Unlicense Rust crate reads and writes them (rpf-archive-rs). FiveM's loader is reference only.

  • Verified No public PDB, no Ghidra or IDA script collection for GTA IV, no CitizenIV source, and no repository at the claimed ElCapor gta4-modern address (HTTP 404).
  • Verified No surveyed source documents the render thread split or Euphoria integration. Both need first-hand analysis.

Names can move from the 360 binary to the PC binary by matching virtual table slot order, the one method that works across instruction sets.

  • Asset streaming. Camera to a registry of 24-byte records, 8 load slots, ring buffers and fixup callbacks. It uses five evidence labels, which this project copied.
  • RAGE API README. The rage:: and GTA4:: class lists. Many entries are stubs, and weapons and pathfinding are listed as to-dos.
  • RTTI and HUD handles, for the method of building class-to-virtual-table tables.
  • Collision aliasing postmortem, which shows the collision pipeline and that RAGE physics is built on Bullet. Inferred for the PC build.
  • Shader pipeline and reflection study, for the renderer phase.
  • Verified Not found: Euphoria notes, script VM internals, a main-loop document. These projects treat game logic as a black box. Reads truncated at about 11 to 16 KB, so several long documents were seen only in part.

Carrying names across by slot order

  • Verified tt-decomp matched GTA IV against Rockstar Table Tennis, both PowerPC, in three passes. Exact normalised instruction hashes matched 0 functions. Virtual table slot position matched 5 of 5, all rage::grcSetup at 85% confidence. Prologue hash plus Jaccard similarity of at least 75% matched 0. The run took 7.6 seconds over 36,409 against 7,161 functions (report).
  • Inferred Slot order does not depend on the instruction set, so it should work from the 360 binary to the PC binary. Instruction hashes will not. No PowerPC to x86 matcher was found. Class names, slot counts, assertion paths and string constants should also survive, but none is yet checked on the PC binary.
